#5086. Tether Gold Gets Clean KPMG Audit Confirming $2.2B in Physical Gold Backing

Tether Gold Gets Clean KPMG Audit Confirming $2.2B in Physical Gold Backing

Tether's gold-backed stablecoin, Tether Gold (XAUT), has completed its first full audit by KPMG, which found the token fully backed by physical gold, the company announced on Thursday.

KPMG issued an unqualified opinion on the financial statements of TG Commodities, which issues XAUT, for the year ended December 31, 2025. An unqualified, or "clean," opinion means the auditor found that the statements fairly present the company's financial position, without reservations.

Tether Gold (XAU₮) Becomes Tether’s Second Stablecoin to Complete a Big Four AuditLearn more: https://t.co/eO0asUwvlI

As of the end of 2025, TG Commodities held 520,089.350 troy ounces of allocated gold, valued at $2.246 billion, against 520,089.300 XAUT tokens in issue, according to Tether. The gold is held in vaults in Switzerland, and each token represents an ownership interest in gold on specific bars.

As part of the audit, KPMG physically counted and inspected every gold bar backing the token, rather than relying only on confirmations from custodians, Tether said.

"KPMG counted every single bar as part of its Tether Gold audit," Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said, adding that he believes XAUT "is on track to become the first true competitor to the gold ETF market."

The XAUT audit is Tether's second by a Big Four firm. In August, KPMG issued a clean opinion on Tether International, the issuer of its flagship USDT stablecoin, in what the company called the largest inaugural audit in history, Decrypt reported at the time.

For years, Tether faced criticism for relying on quarterly attestations, which offer a snapshot of reserves at a single point in time, rather than a full audit of its finances. The company first said earlier this year that it was being audited by a Big Four firm without naming it, before confirming KPMG.

Tether still publishes quarterly attestations for USDT. Its latest, prepared by accounting firm BDO and covering the period to September 30, showed total reserve assets of $191.5 billion against $183.5 billion in liabilities, giving it an excess reserve buffer of almost $8 billion, according to the report. Tether said it made $1.5 billion in net operating profit in the third quarter.

"These milestones advance the progress towards audits across the whole of Tether," said chief financial officer Simon McWilliams.

Separately from the gold backing XAUT, Tether has also built up its own large gold reserves, and Ardoino has said it will keep adding to its stash, which it stores in a former nuclear bunker in Switzerland.

#5083. AI models agreed with each other more than with reality in a new test

Science Prediction Universe found that pooling rankings improved average results, while shared scientific errors survived.

AI models agreed more closely with one another than with laboratory measurements in a new test of AI predictions. Pooling their rankings improved results on average, but several systems could still share the same mistake.

The Science Prediction Universe study, led by UniPat AI and submitted to arXiv on Nov. 11, tested 13 agent configurations spanning 12 models on 100 public tasks and 16 private tasks. Each configuration combined a model, reasoning setting and agent software. The study asked them to rank specified experiments across chemistry, materials science, biology and medicine.

Science Prediction Universe researchers reported that, on the public tasks, average agreement between scored configurations reached a Spearman rank correlation of 0.52, compared with 0.33 against measured outcomes. Agreement between agents exceeded their correlation with measurements on 81 of the 100 tasks. These averages use available scored predictions, with coverage varying by configuration.

Those figures describe how closely orderings match, rather than percentages of answers correct. Agents might rank reaction conditions by yield or materials by conductivity without having to predict numerical values. A perfect ordering without measurement ties scores 1; random rankings average 0.

The researchers found a benefit to pooling predictions. Averaging each experiment's position across configurations produced a consensus ranking that scored 0.08 points above the average submission, improving results on 73 of the 100 public tasks. The reported 95% confidence interval for the gain was 0.05 to 0.11.

On one oncology task, eleven configurations agreed at 0.9 but averaged just 0.27 against measurements. The benchmark’s best individual system also beat the consensus of its peers on matched tasks.

More broadly, tasks with greater agreement tended to have better predictions. The paper's agreement analysis therefore presents consensus as an informative but fallible signal. The authors explain that averaging can reduce errors that differ between systems while retaining common ones.

Pooling rankings improved average predictions in SPU. Comparing the public-task average with one oncology task shows why agreement still needs an experimental check.

Mean pairwise agreement was 0.52, while the mean score against measurements was 0.33, using available scored predictions.

Eleven configurations agreed strongly on one oncology task, but their rankings matched the measurements much less closely.

Agreement contains useful signal, but shared errors can survive a consensus.

Available scored predictions have unequal configuration coverage. The average covers 100 public tasks; the oncology view is one task with eleven configurations. Correlations are not percentages correct. Neither view measures human scientific ability.

Reported public-task agreement and measurement correlations share a -1 to 1 axis. Dot x = left + (correlation + 1) / 2 × axis width. Pooling paths are labelled schematic. Consensus gain is 0.081 score points (95% CI 0.054 to 0.110), higher on 73/100 public tasks.

Available scored predictions have unequal configuration coverage. The average covers 100 public tasks; the oncology view is one task with eleven configurations. Correlations are not percentages correct. Neither view measures human scientific ability.

The authors connect those shared errors to simple assumptions about how experimental outcomes should rise or fall. If several agents rely on the same mistaken relationship, collecting more of their opinions can preserve that error.

The configurations were scored on different task sets. Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 had scores on only 44 and 30 public tasks, respectively, largely because of safety refusals. Across the full benchmark, all 13 configurations shared just 28 scored tasks: 27 public and one private.

The public tasks also looked backward at published measurements and were selected after pilot evaluations. The private set contained only 16 tasks across four unpublished experimental series, limiting how broadly its findings can be applied.

There was useful predictive ability in that private set: twelve of the 13 configurations ranked the unpublished experiments significantly better than chance overall, according to UniPat's Nov. 12 results release. Of 208 official private runs, 159 were scored.

The study used no human prediction baseline. Its findings apply to ranking the experimental outcomes it tested, with lab measurements still needed to check the answers.

#5082. Will Aave’s $21M bet on Bitcoin’s lending potential restore DeFi liquidity or create new risk?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

One of the main metrics to look at is liquidity.

With over 4% of USDT supply being removed in Q4, worth around $10 billion, there is still not enough dry powder to confirm that the market has hit bottom. In this context, Aave’s decision to allow Bitcoin to be used within DeFi lending becomes a lot more impactful. Naturally, the question becomes — Can the move increase capital inflows by allowing users to use Bitcoin as collateral and therefore increase stablecoin volumes?

In essence, could this be the much needed catalyst for a DeFi resurgence?

In a recent development, Aave [AAVE] has gained DAO approval to add support for using Bitcoin as collateral.

The proposal will allow holders to lock up their BTC to borrow stablecoins. Notably, the proposal was unanimously approved on 9th November. This means Bitcoin holders can gain new liquidity through Aave’s $21 million credit market by borrowing stablecoins using their BTC as collateral.

As the chart below shows, Aave will be allocating $21 million to their credit products to five different stablecoins. The two largest stablecoins will be USDT and USDC which have been allocated $8 million each. These account for almost 76% of the total capacity.

Meanwhile, AAVE’s native stablecoin GHO will be allocated $1 million. The last $4 million will be split evenly between USDG and RLUSD with $2 million allocated to each.

Why does this matter? Well, this allocation shows that Aave is looking to blend both traditional stablecoins and newer assets to provide more options for borrowing. Consequently, this will allow Bitcoin holders to borrow against several stablecoin markets using their BTC as collateral.

As Aave Founder and CEO Stani Kulechov explained,

The Babylon-built Bitcoin-backed market on Aave V4 shows how easily new markets can be launched using the Hub and Spoke model. Native BTC collateral, without wrappers or custodians, unlocks a major new source of liquidity for on-chain borrowing and lending.

Crypto lending is slowing down as borrowers reduce their exposure amid market uncertainty.

According to Galaxy Research, the overall crypto-backed loan market fell by 16.78% during Q2, hitting a total value of $56.16 billion. This is the first time that all major lending sectors have fallen since 2022. DeFi lending also saw a sharp fall, with total active loans decreasing from $47.13 billion to $21.94 billion between April and July. In short, traders have lost interest in borrowing against their assets.

However, Aave has seen an opposite trend, with the platform noting all-time highs in active loans on the Aave V4 platform, increasing by almost 100% in Q2 to $500 million. Against this backdrop, the addition of Bitcoin to the lending market could lend further growth potential.

In essence, by allowing BTC holders to use their asset as collateral, the market could see more capital flowing into DeFi, more collateral on Aave, and more demand for on-chain borrowing.

Aave V4’s Hub-and-Spoke architecture provides an isolated environment in which integrations can deploy both standard and custom Spokes without affecting other assets on the Hub.

The crypto market is facing its worst liquidity crunch since the 2022 bear market.

The overall stablecoin market cap has fallen by about $14 billion over the past month. By 10th November, the total stablecoin market cap was around $290 billion, according to DeFiLlama. In fact, the last two weeks alone saw the most net stablecoin outflows ever in over four years. Over half of this drop came from USDT and a further 20% from USDC.

This pressure can be seen across the DeFi space. In fact, the total DeFi TVL fell to around $76.6 billion on 12th November, with stablecoin market cap sitting at $286.9 billion at press time. However, DeFi TVL also fell by 9.7% week-on-week.

Against this backdrop, Aave’s move could offer a new source of liquidity.

There is one technical distinction worth keeping though. This integration doesn’t automatically mean any new stablecoins will flow into DeFi. Instead, borrowers will have access to liquidity that is already sitting in Aave. For liquidity to grow, the protocol will also need to attract more lenders and fresh deposits.

As per the attached chart, there is still a long way to go before the lending market on Bitcoin hits significant levels.

BTC-backed loans reached $3.58 billion in 2025, representing just 0.24% of Bitcoin’s market cap. So, by supporting Bitcoin as collateral, Aave could help unlock this largely untapped lending demand.

Aave’s move could also expose its lending market to greater risks.

According to AMBCrypto, although this new borrowing opportunity on Aave will create new demand, it can also lead to greater speculation. Users can borrow stablecoins using BTC as collateral and then re-lend them into leveraged crypto positions.

Consider this — Bitcoin Futures Open Interest increased by 12.1% in 19 days up to late-October, despite a 5.3% price decrease in BTC. This indicated that traders were increasing their leveraged exposure.

This continued into November, with Bitfinex reporting that this was the fifth time traders added leverage to their positions while BTC fell. The previous 4 times this occurred, traders executed liquidations of long positions worth over $800 million.

For Aave, the concern is that easier access to Bitcoin credit could add another source of speculation.

Ultimately, the move by Aave to integrate Bitcoin comes at a time where DeFi needs liquidity. However, its impact remains to be seen still. While the integration could entice early lenders and stablecoin deposits, there is a risk that high levels of demand could come from speculation and cause further volatility in the market.

Thus, Aave may unlock a new source of liquidity. However, turning that liquidity into DeFi growth will be the test.

#5080. Anchorage Digital’s Stablecoins Can Now Settle Payments on Visa’s Network

Anchorage Digital’s Stablecoins Can Now Settle Payments on Visa’s Network

Anchorage Digital is extending its stablecoin reach into one of the world’s largest payment networks, teaming up with Visa to let select Anchorage-issued tokens settle transactions directly on VisaNet, starting with Western Union’s USDPT.

Under the arrangement announced Thursday, Visa and eligible companies can now use USDPT, a dollar-pegged stablecoin issued and custodied by Anchorage Digital Bank, to settle their obligations on the Visa network.

It’s the first Anchorage-issued token to gain that status, and the companies said the deal establishes a framework to add more of its stablecoins later.

The appeal, Anchorage argues, is pairing the speed of a stablecoin with the backing of a regulated bank. Anchorage operates what it bills as America’s first federally chartered crypto bank, overseen by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

“Speed alone won’t bring institutions onchain,” said Nathan McCauley, Anchorage’s co-founder and CEO, arguing that institutions want “a regulated institution behind the money,” now getting both a stablecoin’s speed and a federally regulated bank’s safeguards.

The move is the latest sign of Visa weaving stablecoins into its settlement plumbing.

The payments giant has built out a stablecoin settlement program spanning networks like Base, Polygon and others, launched a platform to help banks and fintech firms issue and move stablecoins, and has moved into onchain lending tied to its cards.

Dan Roesbery, a Visa vice president for crypto partnerships, framed the USDPT support as giving partners “another trusted, institution-grade option” for settling with Visa.

For Anchorage, the deal advances a broader ambition to become the settlement bank for stablecoins at institutional scale, not just issuing them but providing the custody and settlement rails underneath.

The bank already issues a roster of institution-grade stablecoins, including Tether’s U.S.-regulated USAT, Western Union’s USDPT, Ethena’s USDtb and others, each redeemable one-to-one for dollars. Its counterparty settlement network, Atlas, handles off-exchange settlement, collateral management and cross-border transfers.

Anchorage also recently positioned itself as the custody backbone of the U.S.-Mexico stablecoin corridor, custodying tokens on both sides of one of the world’s largest remittance routes. Backing a token on Visa’s network, which reaches merchants and banks worldwide, extends that institutional footprint further into mainstream payments.

The companies said support for additional Anchorage-issued stablecoins could follow the initial USDPT launch.

#5079. Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks

Home » Interviews » Banxa’s Shaun Heng Warns Rapid Fintech Growth Can Conceal Hidden Risks

An interview with Banxa’s Chief Product & Growth Officer on hidden scaling traps and the future of stablecoin payments.

Rapid growth is often seen as a sign of success in fintech. But as transaction volumes increase, weaknesses in payment infrastructure, fraud prevention and risk management can become harder to spot – and more costly to fix.

Shaun Heng, Chief Product & Growth Officer at Banxa, a global crypto payments infrastructure provider, knows these challenges firsthand. Before joining Banxa, Heng held product and growth leadership roles at MoonPay and CoinMarketCap, gaining experience across two major players in the digital asset space.

In this interview with DailyCoin, he discusses why rapid growth can expose hidden vulnerabilities in fintech, what it takes to build payment infrastructure that works at scale, and how stablecoins could reshape the future of global payments.

– When does rapid growth become a risk for fintech companies?

Our total transaction volume (TTV) grew 76% from January to August. Stablecoins increased by 117%. Great numbers. The first thing I asked was where they came from?

Growth becomes a risk signal the moment it outruns the systems underneath it. That happens more often than people admit.

When volume doubles, every weakness doubles with it. That could mean fraud attempts, chargeback exposure, reconciliation breaks. Just to name a few. So you’re always looking at a great number next to problems that may not have appeared yet.

The second challenge is that fast growth is almost never evenly distributed. It could be one particular partner, region, digital asset, or payment method. That concentration is invisible on a topline chart, so we always look deeper to understand the drivers and future success.

And team culture is real. In a quarter everyone has worked so hard and exceeded targets, nobody wants to be the one asking hard questions.

The discipline I would push for is simple: break down the growth before you celebrate it. Where is it coming from? Which rails is it riding on? And what happens if one of those rails is withdrawn next week?

Growth becomes a risk signal the moment it outruns the systems underneath it.

– What does a payment infrastructure provider need to deliver to make the crypto on-ramp experience seamless?

For a long time the industry shipped widgets, and a widget is a visible admission that someone else is handling this.

Banxa Native is headless by design. The partner owns the interface, the brand, the pricing presentation, the whole journey. We simply sit behind their stack. Users never

Returning users never verify twice, because existing KYC can be reused through token sharing. So, everything the user shouldn’t have to think about. That’s the definition of invisible.

In practice, it means the provider owns licensing, or a licensed local partner, in every market where money actually moves,  local payment methods, not just cards, because users pay the way their country pays.

Vietnam is the example I keep reaching for. We launched VietQR there in Q3, and it is already our top payment method in that region at roughly 42% of all transactions — driving a conversion rate close to eight times higher than cards. Same users, same product, same pricing. The only variable was letting people pay the way they already pay.

Then provider also need identity and KYC, including the ability to accept verification the partner has already done.  Settlement, in and out, with money arriving where it is supposed to on the day it is supposed to.

And it has to run in both directions, not just the buy flow. On-ramp, where a user pays with a local method and receives crypto. Off-ramp, where they sell and cashout to their own bank account.

A lot of products ship the first and treat off-ramp as a secondary problem, and that is precisely the moment a user discovers the money only moves one way.

For a European fintech, Banxa collects the local payment, exchanges and settles the fiat leg where the partner needs it. We carry the MiCA licence that passports across the EU — so they don’t have to build a crypto licensing and payments stack country by country.

One partner, one compliance review, one integration, both directions. That speed to market is usually why partners choose us.

– Banxa’s infrastructure supports stablecoin payments across B2B settlement, consumer payments, and cross-border transactions. What is the most overlooked challenge in making stablecoin payments work at scale?

Nobody has ever been excited about reconciliation, and it is the thing that decides whether you have a business.

A stablecoin transfer settles in seconds. That part is genuinely solved.

What is not solved is everything around it. The fiat leg still moves on banking hours and local scheme rules. You have a bank partner on one side, a chain on the other, and a treasury position sitting between them that has to be funded, hedged and accounted for.

Every transaction has to be matched across those systems, in the right currency, on the right day, with the right fee breakdown, in a form an auditor and a regulator will accept.

The second unglamorous thing is failure handling.

At scale, the interesting work is not the happy path. It is the payment that half-completes.

The most common example is card decline and for many reasons – bank limit, 3D Secure step that timed out etc. In most checkouts that ends the order and the buyer needs to start again, or more often leaves.

Then there are bank transfers that arrive three days late with a truncated reference. The refund that has to go back to a card when the crypto has already left.

Users judge you almost entirely on how those cases are handled, and those cases are where most providers quietly fall over.

We recently shipped Payment Method Switch, which lets the buyer change how they pay without losing the order. It separates the order from the payment, so a buyer can move from card to Google Pay without losing the order or redoing verification, and so they see the new method before confirming.

The third challenge is payment method coverage, which sounds like a commercial checklist and is actually an engineering and licensing dependency.

Supporting the way people pay in the US, Nigeria, Australia and Germany means four different integrations, four different fraud profiles and four different regulatory conversations. A switch only works if the alternative payment method is already connected and live for that buyer.

It matters because this is the layer the user is trusting without knowing it. When the plumbing is right, the experience feels effortless. When it is wrong, it does not feel like a backend issue. It feels like the product lied to them.

– Can KYC be more than compliance — can it actually become a growth advantage in crypto payments?

Yes, and I would go further. KYC is one of the highest-leverage product surfaces in payments. Most teams just never treat it as one.

Look at where users actually drop. It is rarely pricing. It is the verification step.

Someone has decided they want to transact, they have intent, and then they are asked to photograph a document on a screen that does not match the app they were just in. A meaningful share of them never come back.

That is not a compliance cost. That is a conversion problem.

So the advantage comes from three things.

First, verify once. If a partner has already verified a user to a standard we can rely on, that user should not be asked again. Banxa Native supports exactly this through token sharing, so returning users go straight to payment.

Second, verify proportionately. Not every transaction carries the same risk, so it shouldn’t carry the same friction.

Third, verify natively. No redirect, no third-party screen, no moment where the user wonders who they just handed their passport details to.

There is a trust argument too. In most of the world, people are more willing to move money with a platform that looks regulated, not less. Verification done well signals that this is a real financial product. Done badly, suggests the opposite.

My advice is to instrument it. Measure drop-off by step. Iterate. Most teams hand it to engineering once and never look again.

– Crypto payments come with a lot of risk, from payment disputes to fraud. Do you the industry underestimates the value of having someone else take on that risk?

Badly, yes. And the reason is that the cost of carrying it yourself does not show up as a line item until it is already a problem.

The fiat leg is reversible. The crypto leg is not. A card payment can be disputed months after the asset has left. That gap is where fraud lives.

So when a platform decides to run its own ramp, they’re usually pricing the integration work. What they are not pricing is the loss rate, the rules engine that has to keep up with it, the team watching it at three in the morning, the bank relationships that get withdrawn when your chargeback ratio crosses a threshold, and the capital you have to hold against all of it.

Those costs are lumpy and they arrive late.

The real value of transferring that risk is not just the losses avoided. It is focus.

With Banxa Native, the partner owns the experience end to end. We carry the regulated rails and the settlement behind it. They get to spend their engineering time on the things their users actually chose them for.

Risk you have not priced is still risk. Someone is carrying it.

– What’s one thing Web3 companies still see as “just compliance” that should really be treated as a product or growth issue?

Market access. Which licences you hold, and therefore which countries you can actually serve, is usually filed under legal. It is the single biggest determinant of your addressable market.

Teams spend enormous effort on acquisition and then discover the funnel is geographically capped. Users arrive, get to the payment step, and find out their country is not supported or their local payment method is not available.

From the user’s point of view, the product simply does not work. From the growth team’s point of view, the conversion rate is mysteriously bad in half the world. Nobody connects that back to a licensing decision made two years earlier.

The same is true of regulatory readiness ahead of a regime change. MiCA is the clearest recent example.

The companies that treated it as a legal deadline scrambled. The ones that treated it as a product decision kept serving European users without interruption while others paused service. Continuity of access is a growth outcome.

This is also why we think about our licence footprint as product surface area rather than paperwork. Banxa services users across North America, Europe, the UK, Latin America and Asia-Pacific, and is MiCA-authorised as a CASP in the Netherlands. For a partner building on Banxa, that footprint is not a compliance appendix in the contract. It is the list of countries where their product works.

My general rule: if a compliance decision changes who can use your product or how easily, it was never only a compliance decision.

– What development in crypto payments could have the biggest impact on the industry over the next few years?

Stablecoins becoming the default settlement layer for ordinary businesses that have no interest in crypto.

That is the shift. It isn’t necessarily about more people buying digital assets. It’s about companies moving money across borders faster and cheaper, with the stablecoin being an implementation detail they never discuss.

The future isn’t crypto payments. It’s better payments.

Stablecoin supply has actually contracted since May, from around $310 billion to roughly $286 billion. But payment volume went the other way. Allium reported it at $482 billion in the first nine months of this year, up 45% year on year.

Banks, card networks and large fintechs are integrating this into their products right now.

What makes it transformative is the disappearance, not the technology.

Consumers will keep using the apps and currencies they already trust. The rails underneath will change. Identity handled once, not repeatedly. Settlement in minutes instead of days. Fees people can actually see.

In many emerging markets, this will go further and faster than people in Washington or London expect, because the alternative is genuinely slow.

Digital dollars become the practical choice for savings and cross-border flows, not a theoretical one.

Most users will never know a stablecoin was involved. That’s the point.

#5078. Lido’s lending plan could block loan repayments without stopping interest

The lending plan distinguishes a limited freeze from a broader pause that blocks repayments and lender withdrawals. Interest for the paused period can still be added once accounting resumes.

Under Lido Lend’s proposed emergency rules, borrowers could be blocked from paying down debt and lenders from withdrawing. When the pause ends, borrowers could owe more: the next successful interest update would count the time they spent locked out.

The distinction appears in Lido Lend’s November 9 consolidated proposal. The proposed lending protocol, built on a modified version of Morpho Blue, uses a controller contract to permit or reject market actions. It separates a limited market freeze from a broader controller pause. Only the second shuts down repayment, liquidation and lender settlement together. Lenders supply loan tokens that borrowers take out against pledged collateral.

The proposal reports that the core contracts are deployed on Ethereum mainnet, but the DAO would have to accept the protocol separately. Each market would then need its own motion or DAO vote. The forum discussion continued with a signer declaration on November 14; the thread did not announce a completed acceptance vote or creation of the first market.

A Guardian ban stops an account’s new borrowing and collateral maturation but does not itself stop repayment, liquidation, settlement or collateral withdrawal under the remaining rules. The expected first WETH/wstETH market would launch with one contributor-run Guardian and a 1-of-1 quorum, with independent Guardians intended later.

Under the market controller rules, a freeze stops new borrowing, new collateral from completing its activation delay, and collateral withdrawals from positions carrying debt. Repayment, liquidation, lender withdrawals and settlement remain available, subject to their ordinary checks.

The Risk Steward Committee could impose that freeze and tighten defined controller settings through its dashboard, but could not loosen them. The proposed Operational Committee would use bounded Easy Track motions, open to LDO-holder objections, for actions such as unfreezing.

Borrowers can pay down debt, a key consideration when comparing crypto loan terms. Lenders can withdraw available loan tokens or use eligible settlement, which reduces a lender’s claim and a borrower’s debt by the same amount in exchange for collateral valued by the protocol’s price feed.

Settlement is the mechanism behind the Fallback Exits CryptoSlate examined in October. Lenders can exit without available loan tokens, but settlement is subject to market rules and policy limits. Bad debt at the front of the borrower queue can block it.

An Exit Book, a system for posting withdrawal requests, has a separate pause that stops new withdrawal requests and fills in that book. Owners can still cancel requests or use underlying positions directly, but those routes cannot bypass a paused market controller.

A pause blocks those routes. The architecture specification says it stops actions subject to the controller, including repayment, lender withdrawals, liquidation, settlement and direct interest updates. Even a direct call to the core cannot bypass the pause. Vault-share transfers and core functions outside the controller’s scope remain available.

Blocking an interest-update call does not make the borrowing period free. The core accounting specification uses elapsed time to calculate interest, and the controller rules explicitly say a later successful accrual covers time since the last update. A borrower could therefore regain repayment access with a larger debt balance under the applicable interest-rate model.

Proposed controls differ in scope. A controller pause closes repayment and lender exits while elapsed-time interest still counts.

For the banned account, new borrowing and collateral maturation stop. Repayment, liquidation and lender exits remain subject to normal rules.

New borrowing, collateral maturation and debt-bearing collateral withdrawal stop. Repayment, liquidation and lender exits remain available under normal rules.

Repayment, liquidation and lender withdrawal or settlement are blocked, alongside other controller-checked actions. The interest clock is not stopped.

New requests and fills stop in the book. Cancellation and direct core or vault access remain subject to the underlying market’s controls.

A finite emergency power does not guarantee a finite interruption: a separate Reseal path can make an active pause indefinite.

Proposed Lido Lend design, not a live pause. Available routes remain subject to normal rules and other active controls. Interest depends on the IRM. Live market settings and permissions are not independently verified.

Source-bound permission and authority diagrams from the November 9 proposal and current specifications. Arrows identify affected action routes, not quantities or guaranteed execution. No numerical outcome chart is warranted.

Proposed Lido Lend design, not a live pause. Available routes remain subject to normal rules and other active controls. Interest depends on the IRM. Live market settings and permissions are not independently verified.

There is a protective reason to suspend more than new borrowing. The proposal warns that initial price feeds, or oracles, use issuer-published collateral rates, which may diverge from secondary-market prices. If collateral falls in the market without a corresponding rate change, liquidation may become uneconomic and settlement may deliver collateral worth less than the debt canceled. Pausing those transactions can contain that risk, while also interrupting borrowers trying to repay.

The proposed Lend Emergency Brakes Committee has a 3-of-6 signing threshold. Through CircuitBreaker, it could trigger one fixed-duration controller pause per registration while maintaining required liveness signals, called heartbeats. It could not select the duration, extend the pause or end it early.

The roles specification assigns duration configuration and pauser registration to a separate administrator within immutable bounds. The committee’s successful pause consumes its registration, so another use requires re-registration.

The repository’s mainnet profile selects a configuration with an initial pause of five minutes and a permitted range from one minute to 60 days. The first market’s actual setting has not been confirmed.

Automatic expiry also has an exception. The proposal says the protocol-wide Reseal Manager can make a pause indefinite when Dual Governance is outside its normal state. The published Reseal Manager and Dual Governance implementations require an active finite pause and an authorized Reseal Committee acting through the governance contract. That path can replace the finite pause with an indefinite one without a fresh ordinary DAO vote at that step.

These controls apply per Lido Lend market and do not themselves move user assets. Separate DAO-controlled proxy upgrades remain part of the protocol’s trust assumptions.

For the first WETH/wstETH market, watch for the configured pause duration and who can extend it indefinitely. Those decisions will determine how long borrowers could be stuck with an interest bill they cannot stop by repaying.

Chandler Fang, founder of AI payments startup t54.ai, has said that the company's x402 Facilitator on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has processed more than 10 million AI agent transactions. Fang made the comments in an interview that the XRPL Foundation published on X on November 15, and the interviewer put the number of these payments at 11.7 million.

According to Fang, XRPL had almost no transactions made by AI agents three or four months before the interview, which was recorded at XRP Seoul 2026. "The entire volume got ramped up very quickly in the three months," he said.

The x402 Facilitator works as a bridge between AI agents and payments, and agents can use XRP or the RLUSD stablecoin to move money without a separate wallet setup for every agent. Fang said that more than 200 merchants are already on the network.

According to Fang, the most common use case is paying for AI compute. Instead of paying $20 to $200 a month for an AI subscription, an agent can pay around $1 or 50 cents for a single task. "Instead, they can purchase this single compute for about $1, or 50 cents, and it can be settled on the XRPL," Fang said.

Fang said that such payments have low value and high frequency, so the high throughput and low fees of XRPL give the network an advantage. He also expects agent payments to move into real-life purchases over the next few quarters. "We have the coffee shop right outside our booth, right? And we are trying to empower users to use XRP and agent payments to finish a real-life transaction," Fang said.

According to Fang, trust is the main issue for agent payments, and t54.ai's Trustline product focuses on risk management for the financial activity of AI agents. He compared the service with the chargeback feature of credit cards. "So there is no lawsuit. It is a similar experience for agents," Fang said.

t54.ai is also part of Mastercard's agentic payment program, where the startup is responsible for risk management. The x402 Facilitator processes transactions based on Mastercard Verifiable Intent, a protocol that verifies the behavior of AI agents.

Fang said that t54.ai, Ripple and Mastercard are in talks about a three-way collaboration, and the first results will be shown at an upcoming hackathon.

"The ten million transactions are just a starting point. I think next year you should expect a lot more transactions. Maybe even more transactions settled on XRPL will be done by AI agents than by humans," Fang said.

#5076. Tron, Tether and Chainalysis Form a New Crypto-Crime Task Force—Replacing One That Just Collapsed

Tron, Tether and Chainalysis Form a New Crypto-Crime Task Force—Replacing One That Just Collapsed

Tron, Tether, and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis have launched a joint effort to hunt down and disrupt criminal activity involving the USDT stablecoin, just weeks after a nearly identical alliance, with a different analytics partner, quietly fell apart.

Announced Wednesday, the Digital Crime Task Force aims to identify illicit activity involving Tether’s USDT on the Tron blockchain and surface it for law enforcement before criminals can move their funds.

The pitch is a shift from reactive to proactive: rather than waiting for a victim to report a crime or an investigator to flag tainted funds, the group says it will proactively trace criminal networks and coordinate asset freezes, drawing on Chainalysis’s intelligence and AI-powered investigative tools. It will also accept tips and freeze requests from police.

“Criminals are using AI to move faster than ever, and waiting for a victim to report a crime is no longer good enough,” said Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino, noting the company has frozen more than $7 billion tied to illicit activity while working with over 360 law enforcement agencies across 73 countries.

Tron founder Justin Sun framed it as protecting the millions who rely on USDT, which circulates on Tron to the tune of more than $94 billion.

The notable wrinkle is what this new alliance replaces. Tron and Tether previously ran a similar operation, the T3 Financial Crime Unit, formed in 2024 with rival analytics firm TRM Labs and later joined by Binance. Together, the group froze more than $450 million in tainted assets.

But Bloomberg reported earlier this month that T3 was quietly disbanded in late August, with people familiar citing slow response times and a lack of coordination among its members. Its collapse went public just days before the record $6.4 billion Binance hack.

Swapping TRM for Chainalysis is a pointed move, given the two are fierce competitors. Chainalysis has even sued the U.S. government over an ICE contract awarded to TRM without competitive bidding, underscoring the rivalry now running through crypto’s crime-fighting infrastructure.

The new task force says it will target a broad sweep of threats, from romance and investment scams to stolen funds, terrorist financing, North Korean cyber operations, cartel money laundering and child-exploitation material.

The group also framed the effort around a coming era of autonomous AI agents transacting onchain, which it warned will open fresh avenues for criminal exploitation.

#5075. Binance Warns About AI Scams

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has warned of the rising risk of AI scams, including the use of deepfakes that impersonate Binance executives and staff.

The world's largest crypto exchange recently took to X to warn its users that improvements in artificial intelligence are making it harder to distinguish fake messages from real ones.

"AI deepfakes are making impersonation scams harder to spot," the crypto exchange said in a post.

The cryptocurrency exchange has assured its users that no one from Binance will ever reach out to them asking for money or offering unsolicited investment advice.

Binance says scammers are making realistic deepfake videos featuring executives and employees of the company.

Fraudsters are using these deepfakes, some of which are very realistic, to trick potential targets through fraudulent video calls.

That way, people who fall victim to the scam might think they are interacting with real Binance personnel.

Binance warned that scammers often try to reach potential targets through messaging apps such as WhatsApp or Telegram. They impersonate Binance employees by using their names, photos, and job titles to appear credible.

After making contact with a potential victim, the scammer may try to convince them to send crypto, take part in an exclusive investment opportunity, or take other financial actions.

Binance has called on crypto users to be cautious about any unexpected messages they receive, even if they seem to be from someone at the company they know.

A realistic appearance no longer guarantees a person's identity, given that AI can now easily mimic voices and facial expressions.

Users should double-check any suspicious messages through official Binance support channels before taking any action.

#5074. Is Ethereum the “worst asset of all time,” amid estimated $8.83 billion BitMine loss ?

A dashboard shared by trader Flood estimates an unrealized loss of about $9 billion, but applies August purchase costs to November holdings.

Trader Flood, who posts as @ThinkingUSD, called Ethereum a “contender for the worst asset of all time” on Nov. 13, sharing a dashboard that put BitMine’s unrealized loss at about $9 billion.

The image marked the Ethereum treasury company 43% underwater. Its holdings match BitMine’s November disclosure, while its average-cost field is dated August. Applying that older average to the later balance approximately reproduces the dashboard’s displayed cost, leaving its loss figure dependent on that assumption.

Flood cited money lost to hacks, development time spent on inadequate tools and retail losses from betting on Ethereum’s price. He supplied no figures for those categories or comparative data establishing an all-time ranking. His criticism targeted Ethereum, with the BitMine dashboard providing a specific example of treasury exposure.

The image Flood shared listed 6,070,092 ETH, a $3,380 average cost, a $20.52 billion total cost basis and an $11.69 billion market value. Its displayed unrealized loss was $8,829,920,029.

The average-cost field is labeled as the filed average for Aug. 31, 2026. BitMine’s annual accounts reported 5,901,837 ETH at that date, with a cost basis of about $19.95 billion and a fair value of about $14.56 billion. Dividing the cost by the quantity gives approximately $3,380 per ETH.

Those accounts were filed on Nov. 10, but the holdings and cost figures describe the August balance.

BitMine’s Nov. 9 release reported a larger holding of 6,070,092 ETH as of Nov. 8 at 2 p.m. ET. Multiplying that quantity by the rounded August average produces roughly the $20.52 billion cost basis displayed on Flood’s dashboard.

That calculation extrapolates across two reporting dates. It reproduces the rounded total without confirming the dashboard’s underlying methodology or establishing what the expanded ETH holding actually cost. The November release supplies no updated aggregate cost basis.

The dashboard’s $8.83 billion loss estimate is therefore an unrealized mark against an assumed cost. It provides no evidence that BitMine sold those holdings and realized the loss in cash.

Solana is the most vulnerable, trading at $71.89 below all major moving averages, with the $60 level as the closest support.

Shiba Inu has been struggling on the market for ages, and November 14 made things worse: SHIB broke below its July low of $0.00000413 and dipped to around $0.0000037.

SHIB mostly followed the uptrend from July to October, but tumbled quickly due to the general reversal of the cryptocurrency market. The bounce from the July level was unlikely to occur naturally, and the zone where some buy orders might have been concentrated didn't hold.

Back in September, the 200 EMA acted as strong resistance that SHIB was unable to break, and the asset has been sliding ever since. The ascending trendline from July was lost back in October.

SHIB is trading at $0.00000391, bouncing slightly from the low. The drop below $0.000004 isn't a guarantee of anything, as SHIB has already been lower in previous years. RSI is moving around 25, deep in the oversold zone. Multiple indicators suggest a retrace, but the overall market picture is grim, to say the least.

According to CryptoQuant, SHIB held on exchanges is worth around $332 million, while the netflow stays negative. In tokens, around 86 trillion SHIB still sit on exchanges. Most of the activity is still most likely fueled by retail investors, as the largest players stay sidelined or are not exposed to SHIB at all.

Shiba Inu volumes are still low, which suggests a lack of volatility ahead. The market is weak, and it might get weaker, though most of the selling pressure SHIB could face has most likely been injected already.

Solana is clearly struggling, and the death cross on the chart is not likely to help it push higher. The volume uptick reinforces the bearish narrative and could push the price even lower. The volume on November 14 was the highest since early September.

SOL is trading at $71.89 after dipping to $67.37, around 42% below its September peak. The correction is rapidly erasing the rally Solana has built since August, and the price is already back in the range last seen in July.

Solana trades below all major moving averages, with most of them pointing down, which signals that the current trend is getting worse. RSI is beyond oversold, and it is not clear where the selling pressure is coming from. We also saw additional injections of capital from whales, so the current downtrend is mostly fueled by capitulation of larger players, though not by institutions.

The death cross we are witnessing on the EMAs is important, but barely significant for the asset itself. It is a mere reflection of market sentiment, rather than anything else. The short-term moving average is falling rapidly, which suggests an extremely negative short-term dynamic.

The blue moving average crossed below the black one at around $96, roughly 25% above the current price. Realistically, the closest "fair" support is the $60 price level, where Solana bounced back in June.

A better time to buy Solana could be tied to an overall market recovery, which needs a stronger market catalyst that does not exist at this point. Unfortunately, there are little to no fundamental factors that can help Solana reach key market levels right now.

Zcash rapidly dived toward the 200 EMA, and the downtrend isn't going anywhere. However, the situation is very different from Solana. A solid support still exists for the price, and the situation is not as dire.

Zcash has a strong foundation, which acts as a bouncing pad for the asset, even though it lost 46% from the local top, when it traded close to $1,700. ZEC is trading at $915, up almost 6% today after a wick toward $800 on November 14. The longest moving average is still moving below the price, suggesting the long-term uptrend isn't broken yet.

The NU7 update, activated on November 6, also made the Zcash network somewhat healthier by decreasing the target block interval to 25 seconds.

The price violated the $1,000 level, and the moving averages are trying to converge rapidly. The convergence of moving averages might lead to a volatility spike. From the momentum perspective, RSI is close to 30, so the asset is almost oversold.

In order to avoid a deeper correction, Zcash must reclaim the $1,000 price level. If the price violates the 200 EMA, our next stop would be the $800 area, which acts as a psychological threshold rather than a strong technical level.

#5071. The Fed could rescue bond markets and still make life harder for Bitcoin

Lorie Logan wants emergency support for Treasury markets while favoring further rate hikes, leaving Bitcoin exposed to tighter monetary policy.

Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan proposed stronger tools to keep Treasury markets functioning during a crisis while leaving room for higher interest rates. Her November 13 remarks separate two potential influences on Bitcoin: relief from disrupted funding and pressure from further monetary tightening.

In the speech, Logan said the Treasury market was functioning very well and presented personal recommendations, rather than announcing an intervention or an adopted Federal Open Market Committee program. She said intervention should be reserved for extreme failures in intermediation; high or rapidly rising yields alone would not justify it.

Her rate outlook points toward further tightening. In November 10 remarks, Logan described current monetary policy as accommodative and called for at least two further quarter-point increases to make it modestly restrictive. She made the pace conditional on developments. The FOMC's October 28 decision had maintained the target range at 3.75% to 4%; her preferred path is distinct from that committee decision.

Her preferred starting point is lending against Treasury securities. The Fed could supply funding at a rate consistent with its monetary-policy target, supporting financial stability while maintaining the interest-rate stance it considers necessary.

Logan also proposed developing central clearing for the Fed's repo lending. Reducing the balance-sheet costs intermediaries incur when passing funding onward could help that money reach the broader market more efficiently during stress.

Purchases would serve a different need. When lending cannot resolve dysfunction, buying securities could free space on intermediaries' balance sheets so they can keep trading. But purchases are harder to separate from monetary policy because they can push down term premiums and stimulate the economy.

Logan suggested holding market-function purchases in a separate account and committing to sell the securities as soon as possible. She argued that purchases expected to unwind quickly should have much less effect on term premiums than holdings kept for years. That would limit the unwanted stimulus, rather than guarantee its elimination.

For Bitcoin, the implication is conditional. Restoring disrupted Treasury funding could improve the environment for risk-taking. Yet further monetary tightening could still weigh on crypto risk appetite, even if the financial system were functioning more smoothly.

An August 2023 IMF working paper supplies historical evidence for that second channel. It finds that US monetary tightening reduces a common crypto price factor through risk-taking, resembling the transmission to equities. That aggregate finding is not a forecast of Bitcoin's response to Logan's proposals.

#5070. 'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit

'A Massive Mistake': Tech, AI and Crypto Founders React to Jensen Huang’s Nvidia Exit

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang is out as CEO after 33 years, and some of the loudest names in crypto and artificial intelligence think the company just made a spectacular mistake.

On Thursday, Nvidia confirmed Huang’s resignation as president, CEO, and board member, and named longtime finance chief Colette Kress interim CEO. The move followed reports of two extramarital affairs, including one involving a businesswoman U.S. intelligence reportedly suspected of links to China, as well as concerns over a reported relationship with an Nvidia employee.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees on Sunday. Nvidia said in a board statement that it had no reason to believe its secrets or national security were compromised, and its independent investigation remains underway. The allegations about foreign intelligence have not established that Huang knowingly provided information to a foreign government.

But even without any leaks, the scandal was enough for the board to decide to let him go.

The market did not welcome the transition. Nvidia shares fell 14% at Thursday’s opening bell; with more than $500 billion wiped from U.S. stocks in a single minute. The company that was once the most valuable in the world has now fallen to third on that list.

Nvidia was already under pressure before the scandal, and Huang’s departure raised a particular problem for a company built so closely around its founder: Who, exactly, can replace him?

Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, the Binance co-founder and one of crypto’s most influential executives, said “it's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.” Bitcoin entrepreneur and former Kraken executive Dan Held agreed, writing, “He shouldn't have resigned,” and argued that Huang’s personal problems should be weighed against the company he built.

It's a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.

— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance) November 12, 2026

U.S. intelligence officials reportedly assessed Alice Huang as a Chinese intelligence asset, but Nvidia says it has no reason to believe any secrets were compromised, and Singaporean authorities said they lacked sufficient evidence to establish that she committed a crime. As of today, no law enforcement agency has presented any hard evidence against Alice Huang.

Anthony Pompliano, the Bitcoin investor and commentator, moved the conversation from the boardroom to the technology itself. “Do not get distracted by the headlines,” he wrote. “Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.”

Open-source AI is essential to the freedom of billions of people in the future.

— Anthony Pompliano 🌪 (@APompliano) November 12, 2026

Surrounding it all is likely the most talked about conspiracy theory in the open-source AI sphere. The ousting was designed to hurt open-source developments, the speculation goes, since Nvidia is one of the leading voices in the open-source movement, which closed-source companies see as a threat.

For Voorhees, the controversy also prompted a practical question. “Is there a decentralized Hugging Face yet?” he asked, alluding to one of Huang’s stated commitments. In other words, the crypto solution to a potential platform bottleneck is to stop trusting a single platform.

That concern is more than a slogan for a founder whose Venice AI business is built around private access to open models. Voorhees previously told Decrypt that the antidote to excessive control over AI was “open-source decentralization.”

Some developers saw a deeper threat in Huang’s departure: the loss of a powerful corporate champion of downloadable AI models, whose underlying parameters, or weights, can be run outside the companies that built them.

The worry is that an Nvidia without Huang could become less willing to confront firms that keep their most advanced models behind proprietary services.

Jun Song, an open-source AI advocate and hardware entrepreneur, alleged that OpenAI and Anthropic had spent millions lobbying Congress to restrict open weights. He pointed to a “Pace the Frontier” campaign and argued that Huang responded by building the Open Secure AI Alliance, ending his post with, “And today, we lost him.”

OpenAI and Anthropic have spent millions lobbying the US Congress to ban open weights.

When they formed the "Pace the Frontier" group to push for strict limits on open models, Jensen stepped up right away.

He created the Open Secure Alliance to fight back.

Look at the list of… pic.twitter.com/OeasotcLO3

In July, Nvidia joined Microsoft, IBM, Hugging Face, and dozens of other organizations to launch the Open Secure AI Alliance, which works on open AI security tools and standards. Nvidia also backed a letter defending open weights against broad restrictions.

The broader conspiracy claim needs, of course, much more evidence. The Pacing the Frontier initiative is a statement from employees at several AI companies seeking tools to slow dangerous frontier development, not proof of a joint corporate campaign to ban all open-weight models or remove Huang.

OpenAI subsequently signed the pro-open-weight letter, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said explicitly that his company had never advocated such a ban.

Other posts on social media showed how much anxiety the debate had generated. A commenter replied to Song that they were now “counting on Huawei and Deepseek for the very survival of the OSS community.”

Huawei and Deepseek are two major Chinese companies, known for their open-source developments

I can't believe now I am counting on Huawei and Deepseek for the very survival of the OSS community. What a loss...

— Look4Newways (@sflk2026) November 12, 2026

The issue comes with a rather large business backdrop. Nvidia agreed in September to acquire the open-source AI repository Hugging Face for roughly $12.9 billion, subject to regulatory clearance, in a deal expected to close in the first half of 2027.

That arrangement could put both the hardware used to build AI and the largest hub used to distribute open models under one company’s influence—arguably, the most powerful company on earth.

Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney was among the highest-profile tech executives to condemn the exit. “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity,” he wrote, praising Huang for keeping innovation moving even as Nvidia grew into an enormous company.

A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity. Jensen founded and ran one of the few companies to reach a massive scale while driving massive continued innovation and ubiquity, while others fell into the trap of ever-increasing extraction. https://t.co/AkS5XT9HF8

— Tim Sweeney (@TimSweeneyEpic) November 12, 2026

Perplexity AI co-founder and CEO Aravind Srinivas took a more personal approach. “Thank you Jensen Huang for 33 years of bold leadership,” he wrote. He also credited Huang’s generosity toward other founders, including himself, for helping shape the future of American AI.

Peter Steinberger, creator of the open-source OpenClaw agent and now at OpenAI, argued that the decision felt rushed. “If that spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” he wrote on X. “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.”

If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal. Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.

— Peter Steinberger (@steipete) November 12, 2026

Financial commentator The Kobeissi Letter had urged the board to consult shareholders before any decision, arguing that there was no obvious replacement and citing research on the costs of ousting successful CEOs. After the announcement, the account called the resignation “the most costly mistake of the AI Revolution.”

Former DWS executive and corporate-governance critic Desiree Fixler invoked directors’ fiduciary duty, saying the board should protect shareholders instead of indulging what she called a media frenzy.

In general, most of the reactions were supportive, separating personal affairs from business. The corporate espionage angle has apparently not swayed tech enthusiasts.

This Jensen Huang thing is so ugly. Guy takes a company from zero to absolute pinnacle, through blood, sweat, and tears, a pure founder’s founder, great products, makes so many people rich beyond their imaginations, champions open free local AI, and then the incumbent modern…

— Neil Woodfine (@nwoodfine) November 12, 2026

Not everyone outside that chorus thought the security questions could be set aside. North Dakota Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer had called for Huang’s exit, warning about the risk of blackmail and saying the internal investigation was insufficient. The concern from Washington has been largely uniform: the possibility of compromising pressure against the leader of a company central to U.S. AI infrastructure.

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump has remained supportive of Huang: “He’s definitely suffering,” he told the press. “I think he’ll be in good shape.”

Speculation about Huang’s next job spread just as quickly as criticism of his last one. Responding to an X user asking him to hire Huang, Elon Musk replied, “That would be an honor.”

Nvidia says its board is searching for a permanent CEO from inside and outside the company, with Kress running the business in the meantime. Its next scheduled earnings report is November 17, the first major financial update investors will receive after Huang’s departure.

#5067. Britain to spend £4 billion on grid bottlenecks. Can Bitcoin use the wasted wind?

Flexible mines could use curtailed Scottish wind, but most recent constraint spending paid for replacement power elsewhere. A proposed demand service would start in 2028.

Britain’s grid operator forecasts about £4 billion in costs from transmission bottlenecks in 2027, putting a practical question to Bitcoin mining’s flexible-power pitch: can miners cut costs by using Scottish wind that cannot reach other consumers?

The National Energy System Operator (NESO) published the forecast on Nov. 12. Its latest cost breakdown shows why the answer depends on where a mine connects and which expense it actually avoids.

Thermal constraints arise when transmission lines cannot safely carry all the available electricity. NESO can then pay generators to reduce output while securing replacement supply elsewhere.

The forecast concerns thermal constraints, rather than all electricity balancing costs. It is sensitive to gas prices and network availability. NESO estimates costs would be 16% lower without network outages, although those outages also enable reinforcement intended to ease future bottlenecks.

In its Nov. 9 outturn explanation, NESO reported total balancing costs of about £3 billion for 2025/26, including roughly £2 billion for thermal constraints. A little under £500 million was paid to wind farms to turn down.

Around 75% of thermal constraint costs paid for replacement energy, predominantly from gas units.

Scotland nevertheless presents a potential use case. NESO says 28% of wind in the northern area above a transmission boundary known as B6 was curtailed in 2025/26, compared with 13% across Great Britain.

A flexible mine could reduce wind turn-down costs by consuming otherwise curtailed electricity at a connection and time that helps manage the relevant bottleneck. But adding northern demand does not itself deliver more power south. While the boundary remains binding and southern demand is unchanged, replacement supply remains necessary there.

That limits the savings claim: reduced wind turn-down does not establish an equivalent reduction in gas generation, consumer bills or emissions.

Illustration: mining uses some surplus behind a binding boundary; replacement supply still serves unchanged southern demand.

A local mine may reduce wind turn-down costs while replacement supply is still needed beyond the bottleneck.

The 2025/26 share is not a 2027 breakdown. Mining state is conditional on suitable connection, timing and dispatch. No Bitcoin-specific approval, payment entitlement, gas saving or consumer benefit is established.

The share strip represents NESO’s approximate 75% replacement-energy share for 2025/26. State diagrams are qualitative illustrations of a binding boundary with unchanged southern demand, not observed UK mining operations. No savings or generation volumes are calculated.

The Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance’s mining survey offers evidence that miners can adjust consumption. Respondents reported curtailing 888 GWh of electrical load during 2023. That measures demand turned down, while absorbing surplus Scottish wind would require demand to turn up at the right location and time.

The survey covered 49 firms representing 48% of Bitcoin’s network hashrate at collection, with activity concentrated in North America. It does not establish profitable intermittent mining in Britain. Electricity accounted for more than 80% of surveyed miners’ cash-based operating expenses.

NESO’s November thermal constraints report identifies additional flexible demand in constrained areas as a mitigation. Its March 5 proposed Demand for Constraints design focused on Scottish boundaries. It contemplated registration and dispatch through the Balancing Mechanism, NESO’s system for directing electricity supply and demand in real time, with routes for both new connections and existing assets creating additional flexible demand. The March design proposed service deliveries from 2028, after the year covered by the forecast. It did not establish a Bitcoin-specific approval or payment entitlement.

For a mine, a usable connection, service qualification and enough operating hours to cover costs would all matter. For consumers, the relevant comparison is the expense actually avoided after accounting for the costs the project adds.

NESO’s test is overall system cost. The roughly £4 billion forecast identifies the scale of a grid problem; it does not price a mining solution.

#5065. Robots now run AI-written code without an AI calling the shots, succeeding 92% of the time

Robots completed 221 of 240 trials using Claude-written programs for tasks such as uncapping bottles. Human help was available during development, not execution.

Robot programs developed by Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 coding agent completed 221 of 240 physical evaluation trials, ACE-CaP-0 researchers reported in a study posted November 12. The result shows that task-specific skills can persist in code and run without the coding agent choosing each action.

The researchers behind ACE-CaP-0, a method for developing robot control programs, reported a 92.1% success rate across eight tasks. Each program was frozen before 30 separate evaluation trials, with no further updates. Human guidance and demonstrations were available during development.

The experiment separates program development from repeated execution. The agent's work produced a program that could be used repeatedly. During evaluation, that program still used perception and control systems to respond to observations, while its decision rules stayed fixed. Neither a human nor the coding agent remained in the execution loop.

ACE-CaP-0 separates assisted program development from repeated execution with live perception and control.

Human assistance is available during development; the frozen task program runs without a human or coding agent in the execution loop.

Authors' preprint account. Development permits human assistance; demonstration-collection resets are excluded from the ten-reset budget. Repeated execution on tested tasks does not establish reuse under new conditions.

Source-bound qualitative process diagram from sections 2 to 4. Arrows show code revision and runtime sensing relationships, not timing, trial quantities or comparative efficiency.

Authors' preprint account. Development permits human assistance; demonstration-collection resets are excluded from the ten-reset budget. Repeated execution on tested tasks does not establish reuse under new conditions.

Author-reported successful trials out of 30 for each frozen program. These were physical evaluation trials, separate from development; Table 1, November 12 preprint.

The physical setup used two Agilex PIPERX arms and three cameras. Tasks included inserting a charger, uncapping a bottle and packing shoes. Charger insertion succeeded in all 30 trials; bread packing, the weakest result, succeeded in 25. Mean physical execution times across tasks ranged from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

During development, the coding agent wrote, ran, inspected and revised its code using physical feedback. It could ask for textual advice or demonstrations in which a person physically guided the robot arms. Those demonstrations supplied video, arm trajectories and key joint poses.

Development allowed at most ten human-assisted scene resets per task. Resets used to collect demonstrations were excluded, and the budget counted scene resets rather than all robot executions or demonstrations.

The agent could also use simulated experiments when they helped resolve a development question. In a charger-insertion comparison, on-demand simulation produced a program with 100% evaluation success, versus 86.7% for development without simulation. The comparison used one development run per condition.

That comparison also illustrates a cost trade-off. Development took 2.6 hours with on-demand simulation versus 3.7 hours without it, while output-token usage increased from 730,000 to 1,090,000. The time and token figures leave total development costs unresolved; the researchers call for accounting that includes demonstration effort.

Repeating evaluation trials measures how the resulting program performs. Establishing how consistently the development process produces an equally capable program requires separate development runs across tasks.

ACE-CaP-0 leaves behind task-specific programs that can execute repeatedly with fresh observations and fixed decision rules. The study provides evidence for that form of skill reuse after human-assisted development. Testing those routines under new conditions is the next step toward establishing how broadly they can be reused.

#5063. Illinois Crypto Tax Draws Unlikely Alliance of DOJ, Banks and DeFi

Illinois Crypto Tax Draws Unlikely Alliance of DOJ, Banks and DeFi

An unusually broad coalition, spanning the U.S. Justice Department, Wall Street’s biggest lobby, the national Chamber of Commerce and a who’s-who of crypto firms, has thrown its weight behind a legal challenge to Illinois’ first-of-its-kind tax on digital asset transactions.

The groups filed briefs this month in Illinois state court supporting a lawsuit from the Crypto Council for Innovation and the Blockchain Association, which are asking a judge to strike down the state’s Digital Asset Tax Act and permanently block its enforcement.

The tax imposes a 0.2% levy on the full value of a digital asset every time an Illinois customer trades, transfers, or stores it through a broker, even when there’s no sale, gain, or change in ownership.

Critics have called it among the most punitive crypto taxes in the country, in part because Illinois imposes no comparable tax on dollars, gold, stocks or any other asset, and no other state has anything like it.

On Nov. 6, the Justice Department filed a statement of interest arguing the tax undermines federal policy and U.S. leadership in digital assets, calling it vague and discriminatory for singling out crypto for treatment no other asset faces.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, which represents hundreds of broker-dealers, banks and asset managers, filed an amicus brief warning the tax reaches well beyond crypto-native platforms to the traditional banks, custodians and advisers increasingly offering digital asset products.

A separate brief filed Nov. 11 brought together crypto’s heavy hitters, led by the DeFi Education Fund, Andreessen Horowitz, Paradigm and Uniswap, and including Aave Labs, Chainlink Labs, Solana Policy Institute, Phantom, Jito Labs, Multicoin Capital and Stand With Crypto.

Their filing argues the law’s definitions are so vague they could stretch to software developers and decentralized protocols that hold no customer funds and have no way to identify users or know where a transaction occurred. The brief noted an estimated 2.64 million Illinoisans hold digital assets, the fifth-highest total of any state.

“This tax is unclear, discriminatory, unconstitutional, and harmful to the future of finance,” CCI CEO Ji Hun Kim and Blockchain Association executive Ashok Pinto said in a joint statement.

The challenge dates to August. As Decrypt reported, Illinois agreed in October to pause the tax until July 1, 2027, buying time for the court fight now underway.

#5061. Bitcoin now looks cheap by one measure after $1 billion in ETF outflows

Bitcoin’s valuation signal looks cheaper, but five completed ETF sessions lost $1 billion. A durable recovery still needs buyers.

Bitcoin's latest on-chain valuation alert has arrived after five consecutive sessions of net redemptions from US spot exchange-traded funds, highlighting a lower valuation before the demand evidence confirms that buyers are absorbing supply.

CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost reported on Nov. 15 that Bitcoin's market-value-to-realized-value ratio, or MVRV, had fallen below 1.2. The ratio compares Bitcoin's market value with the value of coins at their last-moved prices. He called it the third trigger of his valuation preset during the 2026 bear market. Yet five completed ETF sessions through Nov. 13 recorded combined net outflows of $1 billion, according to Farside Investors.

The alert identifies a gap between lower valuation and returning demand. A lower aggregate valuation does not show whether new buying can absorb coins being moved at a loss.

CryptoSlate’s Bitcoin page showed $65,461 in a snapshot captured at 10:44 UTC on Nov. 15. The page said its price had refreshed about five minutes earlier.

MVRV divides market capitalization by realized capitalization, which values coins at the prices when they last moved. It compares today's aggregate market value with an on-chain cost proxy.

Darkfost identified earlier alerts in February, when Bitcoin had crossed $60,000, and June to July, when it reached $57,000. He also said the preset is adjusted over time to reflect MVRV's long-term decline.

That adjustment matters to the historical comparison. The post does not supply a threshold-change history or reproducible backtest showing what followed each signal. Three alerts within a bear market do not establish three durable bottoms.

CryptoQuant's methodology guide discusses MVRV below 1 as a possible-bottom region. That is distinct from Darkfost's adjusted sub-1.2 alert.

Unlike the specific holder-cost cluster examined in CryptoSlate's Nov. 14 coverage, MVRV covers Bitcoin's aggregate valuation. Both use last-movement information, which records historical positioning rather than current buying.

A separate CryptoQuant note from XWIN Japan, available on Nov. 15, cited a spent output profit ratio, or SOPR, near 0.98. The note did not identify the variant or exact observation time, limiting comparisons with other SOPR readings.

SOPR compares the aggregate dollar value of spent outputs when they move with their value when created. Below 1 means the measured outputs moved at an aggregate loss. It does not establish that every transfer was an exchange sale.

Adjusted SOPR excludes outputs younger than one hour, while long- and short-term-holder versions separate older and newer coins around a 155-day boundary. Those series need to remain distinct when assessing whether loss realization is easing.

Demand offers a separate test. Farside Investors recorded $185 million in net outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs on Nov. 13. That capped five consecutive sessions of net withdrawals from Nov. 9 through Nov. 13.

These are dated fund flows, not Sunday transactions, and ETFs represent only one channel of Bitcoin demand. Still, continuing redemptions leave that channel withdrawing capital rather than supplying the recurring inflows that would strengthen a recovery case.

Conditional illustration: continued loss realization and weak recurring demand would leave the bottom interpretation unconfirmed.

Conditional illustration: sustained SOPR above 1 together with recurring spot buying and renewed ETF inflows would strengthen the absorption case.

Valuation can improve before buyers demonstrate sustained absorption.

Darkfost's preset changes over time. XWIN Japan's note does not specify the SOPR variant or exact sample time. Transfers need not be sales. Conditional improvement would strengthen an interpretation, not guarantee a bottom.

XWIN Japan argued that a more convincing recovery would combine SOPR holding above 1 with renewed spot demand, ETF inflows and healthier liquidity. Sustained improvement in a consistently defined SOPR series alongside recurring buying would be stronger evidence of absorption than a single valuation alert. Continued losses and repeated ETF redemptions would weaken that interpretation.

Nvidia's scheduled Nov. 17 results provide a near-term risk test. The company plans to release results around 1:20 p.m. Pacific and hold its call at 2 p.m. Pacific.

Nvidia’s results could affect appetite for risk assets, including Bitcoin. The test afterward is whether spot buying and ETF inflows return alongside improving spent-output profitability.
