#5024. Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy made $19.53 billion in profit last quarter. Yet MSCI, one of the world’s biggest providers of stock indexes, has decided Michael Saylor’s Bitcoin company no longer belongs in some of its major investment benchmarks.

MSCI’s November review lists “STRATEGY A”—the company’s MSTR shares—for deletion from the MSCI USA Index after trading closes November 30. That also removes the stock from broader indexes that include U.S. companies, such as the MSCI World and MSCI All Country World indexes.

That sounds technical, but the distinction matters: MSCI is not removing Strategy from the Nasdaq stock exchange, shutting down its business, or making it sell Bitcoin. It is taking MSTR out of stock lists that investment funds use to decide which companies to own.

Consider an ETF designed to copy the MSCI USA Index. When MSTR disappears from the list, the fund generally has to sell its shares, regardless of whether the fund manager likes Saylor’s strategy.

This is why it’s bad news for Strategy. It means less indirect exposition to investments.

MSCI adopted new rules in October for so-called non-operating companies. The idea is to keep investment vehicles—businesses that mainly hold financial assets—out of indexes meant to track operating companies. Its screening process considers a company’s operating assets and other financial measures.

MSCI’s deletion list does not spell out exactly which tests Strategy failed. The company, however, argues that raising capital, managing its Bitcoin treasury and issuing financial products amount to a genuine operating business.

In an August letter to MSCI, Strategy called the proposal “discriminatory, arbitrary, and misguided.” It argued that MSCI should be a “mirror of the market, not an arbiter of it.”

Strategy also maintains a software business, but Bitcoin now dominates its finances. The disagreement is whether its Bitcoin activity counts as running a company or mainly managing an investment portfolio.

Strategy’s latest quarterly earnings show $19.53 billion in net income. But that does not mean its software customers paid the company anything close to that amount.

Nearly all of its $20.91 billion in reported operating income came from a rise in the accounting value of its Bitcoin. Under rules adopted in 2025, changes in Bitcoin’s market price appear in Strategy’s earnings even when it has not sold the coins. A decline in Bitcoin can produce the opposite result.

Its software division, meanwhile, recorded $125.4 million in quarterly revenue, down 3% from a year earlier. Its $477.2 million in revenue for all of 2025 was slightly below the $486.3 million reported in 2019, before Strategy began buying Bitcoin.

The immediate risk is selling pressure on MSTR, not on Bitcoin itself. Strategy estimated that funds linked to MSCI indexes hold roughly 13 million of its shares, or 3.1% of its outstanding common stock. Not all of that necessarily translates into sudden sales, and Strategy says the amount is manageable.

But Strategy has repeatedly raised money by selling shares and other securities, then used those proceeds to buy Bitcoin. If its stock falls, selling the same number of new shares brings in less cash.

So the company would have to issue more shares to raise the same amount—or buy fewer Bitcoin.

That is why a stock-index decision could eventually matter to the crypto market. The exclusion does not force a Bitcoin sale, and it does not guarantee fewer purchases. It could, however, weaken a key source of funding for one of Bitcoin’s biggest corporate buyers.

#5022. Ethereum and Layer 1s Explained

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Smart Contracts, Gas, and Blockchain Trade-offs

Ethereum is a Layer 1 blockchain designed for programmable applications. It uses accounts, smart contracts, the Ethereum Virtual Machine, ETH, gas fees, and Proof of Stake to support decentralized applications and compete within a wider ecosystem of Layer 1 blockchains.

While Bitcoin is viewed as digital gold, an inflation hedge, or digital money, other crypto entrepreneurs wanted to push the envelope further. A few years after Bitcoin, Ethereum outlined infrastructure for smart contracts, decentralized applications, and new financial systems. This guide explains Ethereum’s premise, ecosystem, advantages, and the hurdles Layer 1 blockchains face.

The lesson summaries below give a short overview of the full course content. Take the full interactive Ethereum & Layer 1s 101 course to explore each lesson in more depth through guided explanations, examples, and activities.

Positions Ethereum as the next step after Bitcoin, adding smart contracts, decentralized applications, and new approaches to Layer 1 design.

Explains how Ethereum made blockchains programmable through smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Covers externally owned accounts, contract accounts, account balances, Bitcoin’s UTXO contrast, and the Ethereum Virtual Machine.

Shows how Ethereum supports automated financial services such as trading, lending, borrowing, and collateral management.

Introduces ETH, gas, gwei, network congestion, base and priority fees, and the role of EIP-1559.

Explains Ethereum’s move away from Proof of Work and the roles of validators, staking, and slashing.

Lesson 6 - Ethereum Improvement Proposals

Describes how EIPs move from a documented idea through public review and possible network implementation.

Compares Ethereum with other Layer 1 and Layer 0 designs through the blockchain trilemma.

Connects native tokens and blockspace to validator incentives, wallets, RPC nodes, oracles, and other Web3 infrastructure.

Introduces the scalability problem and explains why Layer 2 systems are the natural next topic.

Bitcoin proved that a decentralized network could maintain money and a transaction ledger without a central authority. Ethereum extended that idea by making the blockchain programmable. Instead of only transferring value, Ethereum made it possible to run code on-chain.

The core innovation is the smart contract: a piece of code that runs on a blockchain and automatically executes predefined actions when specific conditions are met. In the vending-machine analogy, you insert money, and the machine dispenses your snack without needing human intervention.

Smart contracts make decentralized applications, or dApps, possible. These applications function without traditional intermediaries, with use cases that range from financial services to games.

To understand how a vending machine can live inside a blockchain, start with Ethereum’s accounts. Ethereum has two main account types. Externally owned accounts, or EOAs, are user-controlled accounts secured by a private key. They can send and receive ETH, interact with smart contracts, and initiate transactions.

Contract accounts are controlled by smart-contract code, not private keys. They cannot initiate transactions on their own. Instead, they act in response to transactions sent by EOAs or other contracts, executing predefined code when triggered.

Ethereum also uses an account-based model, where balances are stored directly in accounts, similar to a bank ledger. This differs from Bitcoin’s UTXO model, which tracks individual transaction outputs. The account-based approach makes it easier for smart contracts to check balances and interact with users or other contracts.

Smart contracts execute inside a virtual environment called the Ethereum Virtual Machine, or EVM. The EVM resembles a universal translation service: just as a translation service helps everyone in a multilingual meeting understand the same message, the EVM provides a framework where smart contracts run the same way on every node in the network.

That consistency matters because every participating node needs to agree on what the smart contract did. Ethereum’s application-focused account model and the EVM together power decentralized applications, including the broader ecosystem of decentralized finance.

Ethereum’s infrastructure was not set up this way by accident. The aim was to go beyond decentralized money and expand how financial services could work. This is where decentralized finance, or DeFi, comes in.

DeFi aims to replace or rework financial functions such as lending, borrowing, trading, and earning interest with blockchain-based protocols. Instead of relying on a bank or broker, users interact with smart contracts that enforce rules automatically.

ETH, or Ether, is the fuel or incentive that powers the Ethereum network. Every interaction, from sending tokens to deploying smart contracts, requires ETH to pay gas fees.

Gas fees are the cost that comes with every transaction or interaction with a smart contract. They serve two main purposes: they compensate validators for keeping the network running, and they help prevent spam by making every action on the network carry a cost.

Gas fees work like a toll system. Ethereum has limited blockspace, and when more users want to use the network at the same time, the cost of getting into the next block can rise.

Gas prices are commonly quoted in gwei. Under EIP-1559, a transaction fee includes a network-determined base fee and may include a priority fee for the validator. This gives users a clearer fee structure, although the total cost still changes with demand and the amount of computation required.

Ethereum initially operated with Proof of Work, where miners validate transactions by solving complex computational puzzles. It later transitioned to Proof of Stake in the upgrade known as The Merge.

Proof of Stake works differently. Instead of miners competing with hardware, validators are selected to create new blocks, with their role tied to ETH staked as collateral. Staking acts as a financial commitment to follow the rules, because dishonest behavior can put a validator’s staked funds at risk through slashing.

Ethereum Improvement Proposals, or EIPs, are formal proposal documents that describe potential changes to the Ethereum network. They resemble blueprints for upgrading a city bridge: an idea is written down, reviewed, debated, and, if accepted, implemented as a network upgrade.

Ethereum was one of the first major highways built for smart contracts, but as more people used it, traffic jams and higher tolls became common. That opened the door for other blockchain platforms to emerge with different design choices.

Chains such as Bitcoin and Ethereum are called Layer 1 chains because they are base, independent networks that do not rely on another blockchain for operation. Other Layer 1s may optimize for speed, cost, decentralization, developer experience, or specific use cases.

The common challenge is the blockchain trilemma: improving two of the major cornerstones often comes at the cost of the third.

Layer 1 tokens such as ETH are not only traded assets. They play operational roles in paying for blockspace, incentivizing validators, and securing the network through rewards and fees.

Other important topics include Web3 infrastructure: wallets as user access points, middleware such as RPC nodes and oracles, and security/audit services that help applications interact with blockchain networks. These surrounding tools fill needed roles around the base blockchain.

Balancing the blockchain trilemma is difficult. To support broader adoption, scalability becomes a critical problem: without effective scaling solutions, blockchains can become too slow or too expensive for everyday use.

In a city-road analogy, a single-lane road works when only a few people drive, but if everyone starts driving at once, the road becomes gridlocked. Blockchains face a similar challenge when demand rises faster than the base layer can process activity.

Ethereum expanded blockchain use cases by introducing smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Ethereum uses EOAs, contract accounts, an account-based model, and the EVM to make smart-contract execution consistent across the network.

ETH is the native currency used to pay gas fees, which price computation and help prevent spam.

Proof of Stake replaces miners with validators who stake ETH and can be penalized for dishonest behavior.

EIPs provide a structured way to propose and coordinate Ethereum upgrades.

Alternative Layer 1s make different trade-offs across decentralization, scalability, and security.

Scaling is the natural next topic because base-layer blockchains face throughput and cost limits as adoption grows.

This 101 subject is designed for readers who already have a basic grasp of Bitcoin and blockchain terminology. It helps to understand what a blockchain is, why decentralization matters, how wallets and private keys work, and why blockchains need consensus before moving into Ethereum and Layer 1 design.

Ethereum: A Layer 1 blockchain designed to support smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Layer 1: A base blockchain network that does not rely on another chain for its core operation.

Smart contract: Code that runs on a blockchain and automatically executes predefined actions when conditions are met.

dApp: A decentralized application that uses smart contracts instead of relying only on traditional intermediaries.

EOA: An externally owned account controlled by a private key.

Contract account: An Ethereum account controlled by smart-contract code.

EVM: The Ethereum Virtual Machine, where smart-contract logic executes consistently across the network.

Gas fee: The cost paid in ETH to process a transaction or smart-contract interaction.

Gwei: A small unit of ETH used to price gas.

Proof of Stake: A consensus model where validators stake ETH and participate in block creation and validation.

Slashing: A penalty mechanism that can reduce a validator’s stake for dishonest or faulty behavior.

EIP: An Ethereum Improvement Proposal describing a possible network change.

Blockchain trilemma: The trade-off among decentralization, scalability, and security.

Web3 infrastructure: Wallets, RPC nodes, oracles, and related services that help users and applications interact with blockchains.

After Ethereum & Layer 1s, useful next topics include Scaling & Layer 2s, DeFi, Market Structure and the deeper Ethereum & Layer 1s 201 guide.

Ethereum is a Layer 1 blockchain that supports smart contracts, decentralized applications, ETH, gas fees, and an ecosystem of applications built on programmable blockchain infrastructure.

A smart contract is code that runs on a blockchain and automatically executes predefined actions when specific conditions are met.

Bitcoin primarily introduced decentralized digital money and a transaction ledger, while Ethereum made blockchains programmable through smart contracts and decentralized applications.

Gas fees are the cost of processing transactions or smart-contract interactions. They compensate validators and help prevent spam by pricing computation.

Proof of Stake is Ethereum’s consensus model, where validators stake ETH and participate in block creation and validation instead of mining through computational puzzles.

The blockchain trilemma is the challenge of balancing decentralization, scalability, and security. Improving two can often create trade-offs with the third.

An editor checks the facts, figures and quotes they produce against primary sources, and every piece is reviewed by an editor before it is published. Sponsored content and press releases are labeled as such and are not written by our editorial team.

#5020. FutureBit’s Apollo III Bitcoin Miner Hits Micro Center Shelves in Its First Brick-and-Mortar Launch

FutureBit is putting its Apollo III Full Node on sale Friday at four Micro Center stores, the first time customers can walk into a shop and take home one of the Brooklyn company’s bitcoin miners.

The compact home miner, which also runs a full bitcoin node, will be sold in Brooklyn, Miami, Tustin, California, and Austin, Texas, as those stores open Friday, FutureBit said in a release. The four-store launch coincides with the grand opening of Micro Center’s new Austin store, the chain’s 31st U.S. location and its third in Texas.

Customers will also be able to reserve a unit online for in-store pickup, the company said. It did not say how many units each store has in stock, or what Micro Center is charging for them.

Until now, buyers in North America had to order the machine from FutureBit’s website, where the company says units are in stock and ship in two to three days. Putting it on a computer-store shelf lets a customer look at the hardware, ask how it works and carry it out the same day.

“When we started FutureBit, we made weekly trips to the DIY electronics section at the Brooklyn Micro Center to buy parts,” said John Stefanopoulos, founder of FutureBit. “On Friday, someone can walk into that same store, ask how Bitcoin mining works and take home a miner we designed just down the street. We couldn’t be more excited to work with Micro Center on our first physical store launch.”

FutureBit’s own shop lists the Apollo III Full Node at $1,099.99 without a storage drive, $1,299.99 with 1 terabyte of SSD storage and $1,399.99 with 2 terabytes. A cheaper, miner-only “Standard” model starts at $899.99 but does not include the full node.

The Full Node is rated at up to 18 terahashes per second in Turbo mode, at about 325 watts. In Eco mode, it is listed at about 12 TH/s and 150 watts, with noise under 35 decibels. A Super Eco mode is listed at about 8 TH/s and 80 watts. Power can be adjusted from 50 to 400 watts, and Turbo mode is much louder, at about 55 decibels. Those power figures are measured at the board and can vary by 10%, the product page says.

The unit is a 6.5-by-6.5-by-6-inch cube that weighs 6.5 pounds, comes with a one-year limited warranty and is assembled in the United States. It uses new 3-nanometer, American-designed chips, a custom controller and 8 GB of memory, and it includes a built-in solo mining pool. Buyers can also point the miner at a standard bitcoin mining pool. FutureBit says the full node and solo-mining features require an SSD, which is not included in the $1,099.99 configuration.

Bitcoin Magazine covered the Apollo III’s debut in February, when FutureBit introduced the hardware as a way for individuals to run both a miner and a node at home. The point, the company has long argued, is not to compete with industrial mines on cost.

A single Apollo III at 18 TH/s is a sliver of the bitcoin network. A home-scale setup in that range still faces expected times to a solo block measured in centuries at recent difficulty, Bitcoin Magazine previously noted. Even so, a miner running through FutureBit’s Apollo Solo setup found block 973,262 on Oct. 26 and collected the full 3.154 bitcoin reward.

FutureBit, based in Brooklyn, has built consumer mining hardware since 2015. Stefanopoulos has framed store shelves as a way to put more hash rate and more nodes in living rooms. The company did not say whether the Micro Center test will expand beyond the four stores that began selling the Apollo III on Friday.

Quality underwear doesn't have to cost a fortune. Take Uniqlo's Airism Ultra Seamless Boxer Briefs, which clock in under $20 and also fit like a glove. Whether it's a hot day or you're working up a sweat at the gym, Airism pulls moisture away from your skin, making sure you don't feel swampy down under.

Every Sunday at my house is wash day, but this underwear has survived through every last cycle without losing its allure. Our only gripe is that Uniqlo Airism sells out very fast, which means you have to wait for the occasional restock—so get them now.

Cotton is the OG of underwear fabrics, and our testers found that it's the most comfortable knit for everyday fits. Take note: while cotton is pretty breathable, it doesn't do a great job of wicking away moisture. That's why our fashion editors do not recommend cotton skivvies for working out. In some cases, a pair of undies that's 100% cotton tends to lose shape over time and can give a swamp-ass feeling. If you have money to spend, we recommend trying a long-staple or organic cotton, which is more premium and durable.

Nylon is moisture-wicking and super durable, so the fabric won’t pill or stretch out. However, a little spandex (aka elastane) in the fabric helps for movement and extra comfort. Plus, it dries quickly too, so you won't feel sticky post-workout.

Imagine cotton, but smoother and a little fancier. Modal has a silky-soft feel that's light and cool against your skin. Testers say their favorite modal boxer briefs almost disappear under their clothes.

If you're looking to keep your precious cargo secure, then briefs provide the most security. However, if you want to let the package breathe, then boxers are your best bet. Remember: Boxers tend to ride up when you're wearing slim pants, which is why we recommend only wearing them with more relaxed fits.

If you need extra support, we recommend underwear with a pouch or a snugger fit around the waistband. For some men with testicular pain or discomfort, they may want to find a style that fits well and doesn't ride up or bunch, as this could aggravate their symptoms.

Your underwear is the first thing you put on and the last thing you take off, so it has to work with you, not against you, all day long. If it doesn't do its job, you'll feel it, whether it's discomfort, chafing, or overheating.

Think about it: excellent underwear isn't just about looking cool (though that's like icing on the cake). It's about how it performs in real life. Are you lounging at home? Going for a long run? Stuck on a flight for hours? Each of these scenarios demands something different. You need underwear that supports your lifestyle, whether that's stretch for flexibility, moisture-wicking for sweat, or breathability to keep things fresh down yonder.

The best breathable underwear manages heat and moisture so sweat can escape instead of getting trapped against your skin. Many use micro-knit or mesh-like weaves that create tiny air channels within the fabric, allowing heat to dissipate and air to circulate as you move. Others incorporate moisture-wicking fibers to pull sweat away from the body and spread it across the surface of the fabric so it evaporates faster. Some brands even add targeted “cool zones” or thinner panels in high-sweat areas to boost airflow where you need it most.

When underwear can’t breathe, moisture builds up, leading to overheating, chafing, irritation, and odor. Breathable underwear works with your body by keeping things cooler, drier, and more comfortable throughout the day. For Men’s Health guys, breathability makes a difference for everyday wear, long commutes, desk jobs, workouts, travel days, and humid conditions. It’s especially clutch for guys who sweat easily, live in hot climates, train hard, or spend long stretches in the same pair from morning to night.

As part of the Men’s Health style team, led by our Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, I’ve tested some of the best—and worst—underwear on the market firsthand. Since 2015, our team has worn, washed, and stressed-tested more than 100 pairs across every major style, brand, and fabric imaginable, from classic cotton briefs to high-tech performance boxer briefs and luxe everyday upgrades.

Testing wasn't limited to just one body type or fit preference. In addition to my own wear tests, multiple Men's Health editors with different builds pitched in, spanning sizes from small through XXL. This allowed us to see how each pair fit and performed across a wide range of body types, rises, thigh sizes, and proportions—and to flag issues like inconsistent sizing, rolling waistbands, or fabric that only works on one kind of frame.

I wore each pair repeatedly in real-life situations, including workdays, workouts, commutes, travel, and weekend outings. I looked at how each pair performed over time, paying close attention to whether fabrics remained soft without pilling, waistbands held their shape, seams avoided chafing, and support held up after hours of movement. I judged each pair on fabric quality, fit, breathability, odor control, stretch and recovery, durability after repeated washes, and comfort levels ranging from morning to night. Only the pairs that consistently delivered comfort, support, and long-term performance earned a spot on this list. What you’ll find here are the top 12 best men’s underwear options that rose to the top after years of hands-on testing by the Men’s Health team.

Boxers: They’re classic, loose-fitting shorts that are lightweight, with lots of breathing room, and zero restriction. They’re great for lounging or sleeping because they feel airy and relaxed, but that same looseness makes them less practical under slim pants. Fabric can bunch, ride up, and offer little to no support if you’re moving around a lot. Boxer briefs: They’re cut like boxers but fit snugly like briefs. That means they hug your thighs, hold everything in place, and layer smoothly under jeans, trousers, or even gym shorts. They also prevent chafing since the fabric creates a barrier between your thighs—a lifesaver if you walk a lot or hit the gym. The tradeoff? They’re less airy than boxers, but most guys prefer the balance of comfort, coverage, and support.

That really depends on your laundry schedule. If you’re someone who does laundry once a week, aim for at least 10 to 12 pairs so you’ve got a little cushion. If laundry happens less often—say every two weeks—you’ll probably want 15 to 20 pairs. If you’re very active, then consider stocking your drawer with 25 to 30 pairs. Basically, you want enough to last until wash day plus a couple extra for workouts, surprise trips, or the occasional lazy Sunday when you just don’t feel like doing laundry.

A good rule of thumb: it’s reasonable to refresh your stash every six to 12 months, but quality underwear can last longer depending on fabric, frequency of wear, washing, and condition. If the elastic’s shot, they’re sagging, developing holes, or the fabric’s thinning, that’s your cue to toss them. Think of it as a rotation—you don’t need to replace everything at once, but gradually swap in new pairs so you’re always stocked with comfortable, supportive ones.

Every man has worn them at some point; boxers are light and loose and so freeing. They're the classic underwear style for men that feels very relaxed with short legs. This type of underwear is perfect for lounging around the house, sleeping, or wearing under relaxed-fit pants. Also comes in a variety of prints and patterns (hello, personality).

Think speedo. Think upside-down triangle. Briefs provide the required coverage and optimal support while exposing more skin for ease of mobility. Here, there's no risk of leg fabric riding up (because there's none).

Perhaps the most popular one, it's a hybrid of loose-fit boxers and tight briefs, offering a solid balance of support and comfort. If you’re not a fan of underwear that rides up too high, go for boxer briefs that have a longer leg and a snug fit, like compression underwear that’s perfect for the gym. They should skim the leg versus squeezing you too tight.

Like the title says, a trunk is similar to boxer briefs but with a shorter cut—halfway up the thigh. It's best for guys who want something fitted but less fabric around the leg. For some visual assistance, think of trunks as the underwear style that most CK models wear on big billboards.

It depends on personal preference, comfort, and the activity. Here's a quick breakdown to help guide your choice, weighing the pros and cons of both.

Tight underwear (e.g., briefs, boxer briefs) provides better support, which is especially useful for physical activities like running or working out. This type reduces chafing and prevents excessive movement, which can help with comfort throughout the day. Works well under slim-fit pants, as it avoids bunching and creates a cleaner silhouette. If it's too tight, it can restrict airflow and potentially cause discomfort or sweating, especially in warmer weather. Overly tight fits might not be ideal for guys concerned about reproductive health, though the effect is typically negligible with properly sized underwear.

On the other hand, loose underwear is better suited for lounging or casual, low-impact activities since it allows more airflow and freedom of movement. It feels more breathable, making it ideal for hotter climates or relaxed settings. Also, loose underwear can be paired with loose-fit pants for added comfort. This option lacks support, which feel uncomfortable during workouts or physical activity. Plus, it can cramp your style—bunching up under tighter pants and offering a restrictive feel.

If you want to protect the structural integrity of your underwear's waistband, the best way to keep them from stretching is to hand wash them and hang them dry. But given how impractical that is, the second best option is to put them in the washing machine on cold water and use a low dryer setting so the elastic doesn't warp. However, our testers say that most of the pairs they've tried have kept their waistbands' shapes even after several trips to the laundromat. If your underwear's waistband has lost its shape, you're probably overdue to replace it.

Even the best underwear won’t last if you don’t take care of it properly. Washing underwear inside out helps remove sweat and bacteria more effectively while protecting the fabric’s surface. Cold or warm water is usually best, as hot water can break down elastic fibers and cause shrinkage over time. Skip harsh detergents and fabric softeners, especially for performance or moisture-wicking underwear. Softeners can coat fibers and reduce breathability and odor control. When possible, air-drying is ideal, as high heat from dryers is the fastest way to kill stretch and warp waistbands. If you do use a dryer, stick to low heat.

#5017. Tether-backed Twenty One Capital reports $1.09 billion Q3 net income on bitcoin gains

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

CEO Rapha Zagury said fair-value crypto gains are a starting point as the firm evaluates mining, lending and potential share buybacks.

Twenty One Capital Twenty One Capital (XXI) reported third-quarter net income of $1.087 billion, almost entirely from $1.093 billion in fair value gains on its bitcoin holdings, according to an SEC filing.

The Tether-backed company held 43,514 BTC as of Sept. 30, valued at roughly $83,700 per BTC, plus $102.8 million in cash and cash equivalents. Its convertible notes carried $486.5 million in principal and were collateralized by about 16,116 BTC.

Twenty One Capital also recorded a $4.8 million operating loss and $1.34 million in interest expense for the three months ended Sept. 30, the filing shows.  For the first nine months of 2026, it reported a net loss of $186.5 million, reflecting bitcoin's price decline.

CEO Rapha Zagury acknowledged the results but said, "A balance sheet is not a business. It is our starting point."

"We welcome Bitcoin’s appreciation," Zagury wrote in a letter to shareholders. "But gains from an asset we own are not the same as earnings from businesses we operate. Building the latter is our job."

Zagury said the company was evaluating opportunities across bitcoin mining, lending, treasury and energy. The company would consider buying back shares when they trade below the value of the assets attributable to them, according to the CEO.

Twenty One Capital was established with backing from Tether, Bitfinex and SoftBank in April last year, with the USDT issuer subsequently acquiring SoftBank's stake this May.

The company's shares fell 19.48% over the past month, compared with Bitcoin's 16.06% decline over the same period, according to The Block's data.

#5012. Kraken parent Payward posts 66% drop in Q3 adjusted EBITDA, plans US prediction markets and personal finance AI agent

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Transaction volume rose 22% from the second quarter to $353 billion, down 30% from a year earlier.

Kraken parent Payward reported $60 million in third-quarter adjusted EBITDA on Friday, up from $23 million in the second quarter, but down by about two-thirds from the $178.6 million it posted a year earlier.

Payward replaced adjusted revenue with a measure it calls "total platform margin," which also deducts staking rewards paid to customers. Total platform margin rose to $487 million in Q3 from $436 million in Q2, according to the private company's financial highlights released Friday, but fell 12% year over year.

Customers transacted $353 billion across Payward's platforms during the quarter, with volume down 30% from a year earlier but up 22% from the second quarter.

Payward said it ended September with 7.1 million funded accounts, up 7% from Q2 and 37% year over year. Billable accounts stood at 1.5 million, up 9% from Q2 and 74% year over year.

Payward said prediction markets for U.S. clients are among the new products next on its roadmap. Payward Chief Commercial Officer Mark Greenberg had discussed a possible rollout on CNBC last December, though Friday's update gave no planned launch date.

Payward also plans to offer stock perpetual futures through its own CFTC-regulated exchange, clearinghouse, and broker, build apps for local markets, and let customers share collateral across products in one account. It also plans to settle U.S. dollar wires through its Federal Reserve master account, test a U.S. credit card, and fund lending in Europe with customer deposits.

On Wednesday, Payward added more than 200 tokenized UK and European equities to xStocks. In Friday's update, it said it is developing funds built around xStocks, which surpassed $1 billion in AUM in October, and plans to launch xPO, which would let private companies raise capital by issuing shares onchain, subject to regulatory approval.

#5010. Hyperliquid leapfrogs Bybit, Kraken and OKX in open interest as Q3 positions grow 80%

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Hyperliquid’s Q3 revenue rose 22% to $191 million as daily traders hit a record and stock-linked trading volumes surged.

Hyperliquid closed out the third quarter with a record $16.8 billion in open derivatives positions following a July slowdown.

Open interest jumped nearly 80% from the end of June, according to a new report from the Hyperliquid Research Collective. This was enough for Hyperliquid to surpass centralized exchange rivals Bybit, Kraken and OKX in open interest.

Its share of open interest across Hyperliquid and eight major exchanges climbed to 11.7%, up from 9.6% three months earlier.

This came alongside an uptick in crypto trading, with native perpetuals volume climbing from $109.5 billion in July to more than $188 billion in September. Average daily traders also hit a quarterly record of 65,161.

Protocol revenue rose 21.7% quarter over quarter to nearly $191 million, including $17.3 million earned from its USDC reserve-income arrangement tied to Coinbase's role as Hyperliquid's treasury deployer. Revenue remained 36.5% below the same period last year.

Stock-linked perpetuals volume also rose 161% to $153.8 billion, overtaking the commodities asset class in HIP-3, which lets third-party operators launch perp futures.

Wintermute, one of crypto's biggest market makers, has become a major user of Hyperliquid's auctions for early access to trading data, Bloomberg reported Thursday.

A wallet linked to Wintermute won 76% of auctions for the top-priority data slot over the preceding month, according to analysis from Loris Tools and cited by Bloomberg.

The system gives traders an early look at incoming orders, allowing them to change their positions before other orders are processed. Critics say the feature gives larger firms an unfair advantage. Wintermute defended it as a transparent way to compete for speed.

#5005. CFTC’s Selig accuses states of trying to ‘lock up’ prediction market founders

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Chair Michael Selig defends federal oversight of prediction markets as states pursue enforcement and the CFTC presses its authority in court.

Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig is turning up the heat on his criticisms of states' handling of lawsuits brought against prediction market platforms and their executives.

Speaking at the Cantor Convergence conference, Selig called the state suits "really egregious" and defended the platforms operating under what he has long called the CFTC's "exclusive jurisdiction."

"We're seeing states bring criminal charges, essentially trying to lock up founders and CEOs of these companies that are offering lawful products under a federal regime," he said.

The comments come amid a stretch of battles between the CFTC and roughly a dozen states and cities over whether event contracts offered on prediction market platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket constitute illegal gambling. Selig argued that the disagreements should be hashed out in court without threatening executives with time in prison.

"Somebody says it's gambling, somebody says it's a derivative," he said. "That's not something that should be at the risk of going to jail."

And instead of fighting on a case-by-case basis in multiple states, Selig wants to see the issue raised to the Supreme Court in a bid to solidify the CFTC's authority.

"I don't understand whether we're going to have every major CEO of an exchange locked up in a jail cell in Utah, or if we can just go to the Supreme Court and hash this thing out on the merits," he said.

On Thursday, the Justice Department and CFTC sued Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin to block his action against Kalshi.

Louisiana also filed a lawsuit Thursday targeting companies including Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood and Coinbase.

"I am concerned that some of the states are getting very aggressive," Selig said. "We’ll continue to defend our jurisdiction."

#5004. Urologists Have Some Hot Takes on Whether Men Should Sit or Stand to Pee

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

AROUND THE WORLD—and on Reddit—there’s an eternal debate raging about whether men should sit or stand to pee. In the US, the answer seems like a no-brainer: standing. One YouGov poll found that only 10 percent of American men regularly sit down to pee, while 31 percent said they never do this. (There’s even that viral video years ago of a pastor arguing “a man is someone who pisses against the wall.”)

But that same YouGov poll found that where you wee varies. In Germany, 40 percent of guys actually sit down every time to urinate. About 22 percent of Swedish men, for example, sit down every time, but 28 percent sit down most of the time. Entire threads online are devoted to this question, including a hybrid tactic as a compromise in which a guy pees sitting down at home but stands up at a urinal in public.

Looking beyond preference, is there a right answer to take a leak? One study published in the journal Neurourology and Urodynamics tried to give a definitive answer. Depending on your camp, the answer might validate what you know—or piss you off.

Researchers had no issue finding 52 guys to sign up for this peeing experiment. These dudes had no prior health issues and were between the ages of 18 and 39. The guys were randomly divided into two groups that sat to urinate. Then they would stand to pee. The other group did the same but in reverse order. Between each change in position was a "washout period" of 24 hours where guys did their business as usual.

Researchers tracked how much urine came out and how quickly. So who reigned supreme on the porcelain throne? Well, neither.

Sitting or standing to urinate didn’t change how much pee they got out in each session. There was a slight difference in how fast they got to max flow, though. Men were able to reach their peak speed slightly sooner when they peed sitting down, but researchers say this finding was “unlikely to be clinically meaningful and was partly dependent on a single outlier.” Meaning, one guy was pissing really hard while sitting, while everyone else peed at a similar rate and volume no matter what position they did it.

The findings are not surprising to S. Adam Ramin, MD, urologist and medical director of Urology Cancer Specialists. “If you're a normal, young, healthy male, it will make no difference whether you sit or stand to urinate,” he says. “You will have a good stream either way.”

THE FINDINGS WOULD likely be different for older men, especially those with an enlarged prostate. “Sometimes in older men with an obstructing prostate, sitting to urinate may help them to empty their bladders more effectively as they are able to generate more abdominal force to squeeze the urine out,” says Boback Berookhim, MD, urologist at Northwell’s Lenox Hill Hospital.

HEALTHWISE, NOT REALLY. But if you have a certain preference for one over the other, then there’s no harm in sticking with one position. There's some convenience with standing to pee: You pull it out, do your business, and move on. Peeing this way is “likely to save time,” says Dr. Berookhim.

Sitters, on the other hand, might prefer the position because it’s slightly more hygienic. Dr. Ramin says guys are more likely to splash, sprinkle on the toilet seat, or even miss entirely when they’re standing versus sitting. Plus, sitters might be more likely to wash their hands after every use. Men are 1.5 times less likely to wash their hands than women after peeing—probably where they could use those saved seconds.

Beyond that necessary bathroom etiquette, there’s really no other reason to switch up your tried-and-true urinary habits. Dr. Berookhim says he certainly wouldn’t tell a young, healthy guy to change the way they are using the bathroom if they are already doing fine.

Korin Miller is a seasoned freelance writer specializing in general wellness, sexual health and relationships, and lifestyle trends, with work appearing in Men’s Health, Women’s Health, Everyday Health, Food & Wine, and more. She has a master’s degree from American University and lives by the beach.

#5001. House Oversight Chair calls for possible ban on government officials’ prediction market bets over insider trading concerns

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

On Friday, the committee released its findings of an investigation it launched in May on insider trading risks in prediction markets among government officials.

The Republican chair of the House Oversight Committee is calling for new limits on government officials' use of prediction markets, including the possibility of an outright ban, amid growing concerns that public officials could use insider information to profit from bets on the platforms.

On Friday, the committee released findings from an investigation it launched in May into insider trading risks in prediction markets among government officials, military personnel, and those with security clearances. The committee sifted through 1,700 pages of documents and also received five bipartisan staff briefings from prediction market companies, said Chair James Comer, R-Ky.

Concerns in Washington have intensified over the past year, particularly after an active-duty U.S. Army soldier who used confidential information to place bets on Polymarket ahead of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro's capture. Thereafter, others in government have also been found using inside information to make money on bets on prediction markets, including the White House's former teleprompter operator. Political candidates have also faced allegations of insider trading on the platforms.

"Congress must consider additional reforms to prevent public corruption and restore the American people's trust in government," Comer said on Friday.

Those reforms should be legislation that restricts which bets federal employees, lawmakers and congressional staff can place on prediction markets — or an outright ban, the committee said.

"Whether it's an outright prohibition on trading on prediction markets or restrictions on some subset of contracts like government-related contracts, applying these restrictions to officials in all branches of government would strengthen ethical expectations that government personnel should not personally and financially benefit from access to non-public information associated with their work as government servants…" according to the memo.

Congress should also have a role in encouraging prediction market companies and federal agencies to share necessary information to enforce restrictions, the committee said.

Both major prediction market companies — Kalshi and Polymarket — have said they have taken steps to tighten controls to prevent government officials from using inside information. Lawmakers have also begun addressing the issue themselves. In April, the Senate voted to pass a resolution to ban members from trading on prediction markets.

Potent compounds in topical products promise to strengthen hair, hydrate skin, and even buff out wrinkles. It’s time you harness their powers.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

YOU’VE HEARD ALL about the kinda-sorta-illegal new world of supposedly health-transforming injectable peptides. But what’s wild is that topical peptides are totally legal and have long been hanging out in the grooming aisle—and some are actually backed by science. Yes, the right peptide-powered products can soften wrinkles, fade dark spots, and moisturize well beyond the traditional stuff. Are they worth your time and money? Possibly. Is there a lot to unpack before you slather them on? Definitely.

THEY’RE PROTEINS. OR, more specifically, “chains of amino acids that vary in length,” says Carl D’Ruiz, a senior manager of business development at global bioscience company DSM-Firmenich. “Peptides can be classified by the length of their chain—tripeptides feature three amino acids, pentapeptides have five, and so on—or their biological function.” To create peptides for grooming products, technicians either construct them in a cosmetics lab or pull them from natural materials such as yeast, E. coli, or animal cells.

LOTS. BUT HERE’S the thing: Because many brands use proprietary, patented peptides or peptide blends, independent research on specific products is scarce. Yet in general, there is some data to support the use of certain peptides for skin health. Three types of peptides are the most well studied:

“THE DATA IS less robust than what we have for skin, but certain peptides show promise for hair health and can improve density with consistent use,” says Dr. Nakhla. A recent research review found that short-chain peptides, particularly GHK-Cu, improved hormone-related pattern hair loss. The theory is that, again, by improving cellular communication, peptides tell follicles to retain hair longer or grow thicker. Peptides aren’t as effective as proven hair-strengthening ingredients like minoxidil or finasteride. But they seem to carry fewer side effects. (Topical minoxidil can cause itchy-as-all-hell contact dermatitis in some patients; compounded topical finasteride products, which are not FDA approved, may cause insomnia, erectile dysfunction, and anxiety.)

The high concentration of peptide-packed plasma is designed to shrink pores, erase wrinkles, and clear up dark spots.

#4997. Bitcoin Price Falls 14% in a Week to $65,000 as Weekend Selling Breaks Friday’s Low

Bitcoin price crashed about 13% over the past week and traded near $65,600 on Saturday.

Bitcoin price crashed about 14% over the past week and was trading near $65,200 on Saturday morning after sliding to about $65,000, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro data. The move broke below Friday’s low of about $67,555 and marked the weakest level since mid-August, as weekend trading extended a selloff that has followed a stronger dollar and a fully priced December Federal Reserve rate hike.

A week ago, on Nov. 7, bitcoin was trading near $75,750. The decline steepened after Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, a shake-up that caused AI stocks to sell off which could potentially be responsible for sending bitcoin below $72,000. It slipped toward $71,000 by Thursday evening, then crashed to about $67,555 around midnight Eastern on Friday, its lowest level since August, before recovering toward $69,800 in the morning.

A brief pop above $70,000 after the producer-price report faded, and the bitcoin price spent Friday afternoon pinned below $70,000, near $68,900.

Selling resumed Friday evening and carried into the mid-$66,000s. Bitcoin briefly steadied overnight near $67,000, then sold off again after 8 a.m. ET Saturday, reaching that $65,500 low in the 10 a.m. hour and taking out Friday’s trough.

The Labor Department said Friday that the Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3% in October, short of the 0.4% increase economists had expected. On an unadjusted basis, the index was up 6.5% from a year earlier, the largest 12-month rise since November 2022. The slightly cooler monthly figure lifted bitcoin above $70,000 for only minutes.

Bond traders were unconvinced. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed as high as 5.17% on Friday, a four-week high, and closed at 5.15%. The U.S. dollar index held at a 19-month high, its strongest level since April 2025. Boston Fed President Susan Collins said Friday that “soon, some additional tightening of Fed monetary policy may be appropriate,” and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said policymakers will, “in all likelihood, raise interest rates.” Higher rates raise the cost of holding an asset that pays no interest, and a stronger dollar has weighed on the bitcoin price for much of November. Traders fully priced a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting, CME FedWatch data show.

Chip stocks offered no cushion. The iShares Semiconductor ETF fell more than 3% on Friday, and Advanced Micro Devices dropped more than 8%. The Nasdaq 100 closed down 1.22%. U.S. stock and bond markets are closed Saturday, but those levels still frame the weekend session. Nvidia is due to report third-quarter results on Tuesday under interim CEO Colette Kress, the first earnings release since Huang stepped down.

Demand from spot bitcoin ETFs has not filled the gap. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) bled $2 billion over nine straight days of outflows through Wednesday, and the funds posted a sixth straight day of net outflows on Thursday. Weekend trading is typically thinner, leaving the bitcoin price more exposed to sharp swings in either direction.

Miners got some relief overnight. Bitcoin’s mining difficulty dropped 9.13% at 12:02 a.m. ET Saturday at block 975,744, falling from about 148.36 trillion to 134.82 trillion, the largest cut since June. Difficulty adjusts automatically every 2,016 blocks to keep average block times near 10 minutes.

The next tests for the bitcoin price arrive quickly. Traders will watch whether Saturday’s slide holds below Friday’s $67,555 low, and whether Nvidia’s report on Tuesday extends the chip-stock weakness that has followed bitcoin lower all week. With a December rate hike fully priced and the dollar at a 19-month high, any further jump in yields when markets reopen could keep pressure on.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $65,100.

#4992. Meta tests prediction market app using ‘cred’ points instead of cash: WSJ

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Meta’s employee trial advances its prediction market push as Kalshi and Polymarket battle state gambling lawsuits.

Meta has started internal testing of a prediction market app with its employees that would let users compete on guessing the outcome of events without putting real money on the line, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday.

The app, now going by the name Takes, lets users bet "cred" points, according to the report, which cited people familiar with the matter. Similar to other mainstream prediction markets that use money, correct predictions on Takes earn cred while wrong ones lose points.

The testing phase follows June reports that CEO Mark Zuckerberg directed employees to build a standalone prediction market app that would use points, though Meta had not ruled out eventually allowing real-money betting. At the time, the app was going by the name Arena.

The Journal's report does not say whether real-money contracts remain a possibility. Meta declined to comment or give a timetable for a public release.

It comes as real-money platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket are facing lawsuits from states that accuse them of offering illegal gambling. The platforms maintain that their event contracts are legal and fall under the jurisdiction of the federal government.

Speaking at the Cantor Convergence conference on Friday, Commodity and Futures Trading Commission Chair Michael Selig criticized states for pursuing criminal charges against prediction market executives, adding that the disputes should be raised to the Supreme Court.

"Somebody says it's gambling, somebody says it’s a derivative," Selig said. "That's not something that should be at the risk of going to jail."

#4986. The 8 Best Nose Hair Trimmers for Men in 2026, Tested by Grooming Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

This process doesn't need to be painful with the right tool.

IT STARTS WITH a quick glance—a double-take in the mirror under harsh bathroom lighting. Then there it is: a single, wiry hair brazenly peeking out of your nostril like it’s trying to escape. Soon, you’re spotting strands in places they never used to grow, like your ears, and this only multiplies with time. While a beard trimmer, electric razor, or pair of tweezers can help, the best way to keep them in check is to arm yourself with a nose hair trimmer—preferably one that won’t feel like a medieval torture device.

Nose hair trimmers are specifically built to tackle those tricky, hard-to-reach spots. Many models come loaded with extras—think built-in lights, interchangeable heads, even mini vacuums to keep your sink clean. Technically, you could use scissors, but it’s a risk. Snipping near sensitive nasal tissue can lead to nicks and cuts, and as for waxing—well, that’s best left to professionals, not your bathroom mirror. Unless you enjoy excruciating pain and opening your nostrils to infection and disease.

It might be unpleasant to look at when overgrown, but nose hair exists for a reason. It acts as a natural filter, trapping dust, debris, and other particles before they make their way into your body and potentially cause infection or illness. That’s why fully removing it, like with waxing, isn’t a great idea. But those long, visible strands sticking out? They’re not doing the job any better than the hidden ones. The key is balance: trim regularly, but don’t overdo it. Just tidy up when the hairs start to show.

Most nose hair trimmers are reasonably affordable, and shelling out a ton of money isn’t necessarily going to get you the best one. Think about how often you’ll use it, and if you’re mostly concerned with nose hairs or want to use it for other things, too. Many come with multiple attachments to help you tackle errant eyebrow hairs and sometimes even detail your beard. Plus, there are quality nose hair trimmers available at every budget point, so get ready to say goodbye to those long hairs for good.

This is the Rolls-Royce of nose hair trimmers—pricey, yes, but absolutely premium in performance. Its comfortable, well-balanced design lets me use it not just on my nose, but also for my ears and eyebrows. Still, where it really stands out is clearing nasal hair quickly and comfortably. The built-in vacuum keeps things sanitary by reducing leftover clippings and minimizing bacterial buildup.

I also appreciate the wet/dry functionality—it’s easy to clean whether I’m using it in the shower or at the sink. During testing, I found the dual-edge blade trimmed hair much faster than cheaper options, like the Zorami trimmer, which often needed extra time to do the same job. And while the vacuum system is a major plus for cleanup, I did have to empty it about every four months or so with regular use.

Testing Notes: This nose hair trimmer is bulky, per se, because nose hair trimmers are, by default, small appliances, but it is hefty. It sits well in your hand and is easy to hold and grip, which is a surprisingly needed and under-represented feature in the nose hair trimmer world. It’s truly the Rolls-Royce of trimmers, powering through thick and long nose hairs with ease, and leaving your nostrils feeling shorn and clean.

The vacuum is also a very welcome feature that I didn’t know I needed until I tried it. After all, who really wants to clean up nose hair clippings from their sink? The one thing I will say is that while you can technically use this in the shower thanks to the wet/dry feature, cutting hair of all kinds is easier when it’s dry, even nose hairs. I’d recommend sticking to using it outside of the shower.

Long-Term Results: After six months of using Panasonic's Ear and Nose Hair Trimmer, I found that it trims my errant nostril hairs as well as it did right out of the box. The battery life did decrease slightly after six months of using it, but not enough of a decline to make a huge difference.

Battery-powered nose trimmers work fine if you’re only trimming once in a while. But if you stay on top of your nostril grooming (and you should—nose hair grows faster than most people think), a rechargeable model makes way more sense. That’s why I went with this one from Manscaped.

It's not surprising that the brand that reinvented the body groomer delivered the same technology above your neck with the first iteration of The Weed Whacker, but the 2.0 takes it to a whole other level.

It packs a 7,000 rpm motor—the only more powerful option is the Panasonic trimmer, our best overall—into a compact design, and the hypoallergenic stainless steel cone protects sensitive skin while trimming. That means you get a smooth cut without the tugging or irritation.

Testing Notes: During my first time using it, I noticed how seamlessly it cut nasal fur. Even more impressive: it was the quietest trimmer I’ve tried, which made for an even more pleasant shaving experience. Plus, the tip is angled to allow you to reach even the hardest-to-reach crevices in your schnoz.

Unlike most of the other nose hair trimmers on this list, it’s rechargeable via USB, so no need to switch out batteries. Each charge also gets you 45 minutes of trim time, which is the longest on this list. For comparison, Panasonic’s best in-case option gets 40 minutes per charge.

Long-Term Results: After using it for two months, Manscape's marquee nose trimmer cut just as close as it did when I first tested it. Not to mention, its 45-minute battery life still held up after multiple charges.

I get it, building a solid grooming arsenal can get expensive quickly. So if you're looking to trim costs (pun intended) on your grooming gadgets, but still want something that gets the job done, then look to Zorami's trimmer that's less than $14. Given that it's a top-rated rig on Amazon, I decided to try the Zorami ourselves.

At this price point, I was impressed by its waterproof capabilities and a 6,500 RPM motor that slices hair pretty cleanly. While it didn't cut as closely as the Manscaped or Philips Norelco trimmers, it still did a commendable job cleaning our nostrils, only adding a few extra minutes to our shaving time compared to our top-rated trimmers.

You can easily pop off the top and rinse under water to clean. Then, after every use, you can snap on the protective top case, a useful feature for keeping your gadget clean while traveling. The only qualms about this trimmer might be overall durability and lifespan, but for those who don't have a lot of nose hair to battle, this is an ideal starter trimmer to go with.

Testing Notes: When you’re using this trimmer, compared to the others on this list, you can definitely tell it’s an inexpensive version. That’s not necessarily a bad thing; it just means that it doesn’t have a lot of the bells and whistles that some of the more expensive options have. That said, it delivers where it matters—namely, cutting ability.

It’s not as fast as some of the others on this list and, in some cases, doesn’t cut quite as close (those with thicker nose hairs will need to use it a bit more frequently), but for the average guy with average nose foliage, it does the job and does it well. The blades have protective tube technology designed to protect the nostrils from cuts and irritation, making it great for sensitive skin, especially considering the nostrils are one of the most sensitive areas on the face. The nose, ear, and eyebrow attachments (with multiple-length combs) all work well, and the trimmer even comes with a nifty attachment for your sideburns.

Good thing there is a pouch included, as well, because these attachments are tiny and definitely easy to lose at the bottom of your Dopp kit or bathroom drawer. I usually prefer a rechargeable tool, but the replaceable lithium battery is fine and convenient for travel.

Long-Term Results: After using it for four months, I can safely say that Philips' Norelco trimmer still trimmed just as efficiently as it did when I first received it. While it comes with several attachments for shaving the rest of your body, I found that they didn't cut as closely as the original blade, so I’d recommend buying a separate body groomer.

Most nose hair trimmers use either a rotary blade or a dual-blade setup. What really sets the Conair model apart, though, is its distinctive mushroom-shaped cutting head. The lip at the tip lets me guide it precisely along the inner edge of my nostrils, reaching spots that other trimmers couldn't quite get to. Of all the options I’ve tried, this one gave me the closest trim.

While a lot of people—including many of my fellow editors—really appreciate this unique design, some are perfectly content with a standard rotary trimmer. Honestly, it comes down to personal preference, the way your nose hair grows, and how often you find yourself trimming.

Beyond the cutting performance, I also appreciated the Conair’s ergonomic build. Its textured grip gave me better control, and the slim body fit easily into my travel kit—ideal for keeping things tidy on the go. It also includes three attachments for beard and body grooming, but I found those didn’t shave nearly as close as the nose hair trimmer itself.

Testing Notes: Let’s be honest—the extra attachments are fine if you need them, but they don’t compare to the main attraction: the nose hair trimmer. What really impressed me was its mushroom-shaped head. It’s a smart design tweak that lets me reach spots inside my nostrils that traditional trimmers usually miss.

Long-Term Results: After using it for over five months, I still dig this trimmer’s super close cut. However, Conair's motor has gotten slightly louder over time.

If you’re primarily interested in portability, Wahl’s Micro Groomsman is your best bet. This little gadget packs serious power and efficiency while barely being larger than a Sharpie. Perfect to fit in any travel bag or Dopp kit, the Micro Groomsman will ensure there are no lingering nose hairs poking out, whether you’re departing for the beach or the boardroom.

Its sleek rotary head can smoothly manage nose hairs (not to mention ear whiskers), while its detailer blade adjustment can help shape and neaten facial hair. This add-on also comes in handy for cleaning up necklines and other last-minute touchups when traveling.

Thanks to its streamlined design, operating the device was quick and simple—another boon for busy travelers. While the Micro Groomsman is not waterproof, cleaning it only requires removing the stainless steel rotary head to run it under water.

Testing Notes: I primarily use the Micro Groomsman when traveling or for last-minute touchups in a jam, but it certainly has the power to be an everyday nose hair trimmer, especially for those with less thick hair.

Long-Term Results: The integrity and effectiveness of the Micro Groomsman’s design hold up over time; however, the battery life may leave some wanting more. The batteries don’t last as long as other trimmers on this list, which could prove taxing to last-minute travelers. I initially got about two months of regular use with one fresh battery, but it’s closer to six weeks now, so I’d recommend bringing along a backup battery for any traveling.

Sure, electric nose hair trimmers are probably best for daily grooming, but let’s be real—sometimes these trusty devices just can't get rid of that one stubborn hair. That's when a good pair of nose hair scissors comes in handy to take care of those last few strays.

Of all the scissors I've tried and snipped with, the Shears 3.0 were by far the most effective—and durable. Doubling as nail clippers (though you probably shouldn't use the same pair for both), these shears are sharp enough to eliminate any lingering hairs and tiny enough to fit into the smallest of nostrils. Plus, it comes in a nifty travel kit that includes a fingernail clipper, toenail clipper, nail file, and slant-tip tweezers—all of which are stainless steel and waterproof. It’s a mainstay in my Dopp kit.

Testing Notes: In theory, you could use these scissors to trim all your nose hairs, especially if your nose isn’t too fuzzy. But, honestly, they're best suited for those precise touch-ups—like snipping away a few stray hairs when needed. But either way, take it slow. As these were designed to also trim fingernails, they’re quite sharp and can certainly cause a cut if you're not careful. To limit risk, I recommend you get up close to the mirror and be deliberate, so you're only trimming the hairs you want to get rid of.

Long-Term Results: I don’t use these shears nearly as often as my electric trimmer, since they're best for touch-ups or travel, but they still cut as cleanly as when I first tested them. Thanks to their stainless steel design, there’s been minimal wear and tear over the six months I've been testing them, not to mention zero rusting.

Of course, one of the few complaints about electric nose hair trimmers—battery-powered or otherwise—is often their need to be recharged or refueled with new batteries. This Royal nose hair trimmer combats that common gripe by eschewing electricity entirely.

It works by simply squeezing the handles together, which manually rotates the blades to trim hair. The indented handles also help to ensure you never lose your grip and the tool stays properly placed in your nostril.

The Royal Nose Hair Trimmer is specifically designed to avoid irritation by enclosing blades so that they won’t come in contact with skin, limiting the risk of cuts and nicks.

Sure, the process is slightly more laborious, and the cuts aren’t as precise as other nose hair trimmers on this list, but it’s barely enough to notice. That tradeoff may be well worth it for those who are sensitive to the noisier nose hair trimmer.

Testing Notes: Given its manual design, there were times when this trimmer pulled hair rather than cut it. This can occasionally feel like plucking your nose hairs instead of cutting them, but when operated properly with some patience, it usually holds up without much pulling.

That said, cleaning was a bit more involved than the above options, as you have to pop the top off to do so. The device is water-resistant, however, so you can simply run it under the faucet in a jam.

Long-Term Results: As an everyday nose hair trimmer, this one might not be ideal, but it’s a great option when traveling. I found it can also come in handy during those ever-stressful times when batteries or a charge abruptly die.

When it comes to nose hair trimming, or any manscaping, really, the means by which blades will be brushed against your skin is crucial. For nose trimmers, this typically comes down to one of two options: either a rotary or slide cutter. Slide cutters resemble more traditional clippers, while rotary heads are the ones that look closer to a pen cap. While rotary options tend to give a closer shave, slide cutters offer more control and precision since they only cut in a straight, back-and-forth motion.

Given that these devices are made to be inserted into the nostril, most are primarily equipped with a rotary head, but some offer the option of a slide for folks who prefer the old-school feel. Of course, there are also a few with adjustments for both to accommodate the more indecisive among us.

With most products, you might look solely for a long battery life to ensure you can spend less time charging or replacing batteries, and more time using the device. However, with nose hair trimmers, there are a few other caveats to consider, which can impact the overall grooming experience—namely, the source of its power.

Battery-operated nose hair trimmers take up less storage space, as they don’t need a charging mount or cable, but will likely cost more long-term due to battery replacements. On the other hand, nose hair trimmers with wall chargers can be refueled at any time as long as there’s an outlet nearby. Plus, there are few things more annoying than a trimmer sputtering out with dying batteries, which chargers make easier to avoid. While nose hair trimming takes substantially less time than beard or body hair, you’ll still want one that has at least 30 minutes of runtime to avoid frequently recharging.

At Men’s Health, we’ve been testing nose hair trimmers for years now, focusing on key performance factors like trimming precision, comfort during use, ease of handling, value for the price, and long-term durability. There isn’t a nose trimmer out there that we haven’t gotten our hands on at some point, while also paying close attention to common pain points, like pulling, irritation, and inconsistent results.

While updating this roundup with the latest and greatest nose trimmers, I considered past favorites and emerging tools, ultimately landing on over 20 to try or give another look. After testing each for at least three weeks, I refined our findings to a final shortlist: the eight best nose hair trimmers that truly deliver on performance and reliability.

I’ll admit, the idea of sticking a trimmer up your nose can feel a little intimidating at first, but trust me, the best nose hair trimmers are built to be safe and painless. Most use rotary blades, which are tucked inside a cylindrical guard to protect your skin. That design helps prevent snags and, thankfully, those awful little nicks that hurt way more than they should.

When I trim, I gently place the device just inside one nostril, switch it on, and slowly rotate it to catch as many hairs as possible. There’s no need to push it too far—keeping it shallow is safer and more effective. I usually listen for the sound of hair being cut, and once it goes quiet, I move on to the other nostril.

Some trimmers also come with a slide cutter, which I’ve found more useful for shaping sideburns or cleaning up my neckline. That said, if you’ve got extra-long hairs in your nose or ears, you can carefully trim them down with the slide cutter before switching back to the rotary head for a closer finish.

Also, rest assured that this process isn’t painful with the right tool. Even if you have really long or thick nostril hairs, using a nose hair trimmer won’t hurt. The blades aren’t shaving the hairs down to the skin—they’re just cutting them to a length so they won’t stick out of your nose. Think of it the same as getting a haircut.

Despite their relatively low price, it can still be hard to justify a tool for such a specific issue. Luckily, you can use a nose hair trimmer in some other places. Even the simplest ones are good for ear and eyebrow hairs.

Some other trimmers also come with interchangeable attachments to help shape facial hair and trim mustaches, beards, and sometimes body hair. But keep in mind that if you use an attachment for your nose, you shouldn’t use it anywhere else to avoid cross-contamination. Even if you wash it off thoroughly, it’s a risk.

Still, others are full-on clippers with a nose hair trimmer attachment. Choose one depending on where you want to use it, but don’t try to go rogue. Stick to what the trimmer and attachments are designed for.

#4985. Bitcoin ETFs lose $1 billion for the second week in a row as crypto funds, except one, continue bleeding

The 12 U.S. spot bitcoin funds have lost $1.91 billion over seven straight trading days, and no other crypto ETF categories, save one, saw any net inflows last week.

U.S. spot bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) ETFs saw $1.07 billion in net outflows last week, their second straight week with more than $1 billion leaving the funds, per The Block's analysis of SoSoValue data. The last time the funds posted back-to-back $1 billion outflow weeks was in late May and early June.

The selling stretched to nearly every crypto ETF category. Of the 15 groups of U.S. spot crypto funds tracked by SoSoValue, 10 posted net outflows last week and four reported no flows at all. Avalanche Avalanche (AVAX) funds were the only category with a weekly inflow, taking in a minute $227,000 on Thursday. Overall, U.S. spot crypto ETFs saw about $1.55 billion in total leave the funds.

The bitcoin funds saw outflows in all five days last week. They lost $201.1 million on Monday, $95 million on Tuesday, $299.9 million on Wednesday, $284 million on Thursday and $185.5 million on Friday.

Combined with the $1.28 billion that left the funds the week before, bitcoin ETFs have now shed $2.35 billion over two weeks. That is the largest two-week total since the fortnight ending June 5, when the funds lost $3.14 billion.

Friday's outflow was the bitcoin funds' seventh consecutive daily loss, a losing streak that has drained $1.91 billion from the funds since it began Nov. 5. It is the longest daily outflow streak since the 10-session stretch from June 17 to July 1, which drained about $2.71 billion, as The Block reported at the time.

BlackRock's IBIT accounted for $143.5 million of Friday's outflows, or about 77% of the total, per SoSoValue. Fidelity's FBTC lost $41.9 million, and the other 10 funds reported no flows. IBIT currently holds bitcoin worth $53.99 billion against $64.19 billion in cumulative inflows since launch.

Bitcoin ETFs have come to lose $2.35 billion in November after nine trading days, already their largest monthly outflow since June, when $4.51 billion left the funds. They are now down about $1.98 billion for 2026, more than double the $914.1 million deficit they carried a week earlier after flipping negative for the year.

The outflows came as bitcoin dropped below $69,000 early Friday, its lowest level since Aug. 20 at the time, as traders weighed Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO and expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike, as The Block reported. The world's most valuable cryptocurrency fell further on Saturday morning, currently trading around $65,650, per The Block's Bitcoin price page.

Spot ether Ethereum (ETH) ETFs lost $398.9 million last week, per SoSoValue, their seventh consecutive negative week; the category has twice posted eight-week outflow streaks, most recently when it matched that record in early July, so another negative week would tie it again.

The seven-week losing streak has pulled about $2.42 billion from the funds since late September, per SoSoValue's data. Monday's $184.5 million outflow was last week's largest, followed by $144.8 million on Wednesday and $70.6 million on Thursday.

A minuscule $2.4 million inflow on Friday ended a six-trading-day outflow streak worth $594.4 million. Fidelity's FETH drew $11.6 million that day, offsetting a $9.3 million outflow from Grayscale's Ethereum Mini Trust, while BlackRock's ETHA reported no flows.

Ether ETFs are now down about $804.5 million for 2026, nearly double the $405.6 million deficit from a week earlier. Net assets fell 15.5% over the week to $10.85 billion, their lowest since Aug. 18 and about $670 million below the funds' $11.52 billion in cumulative net inflows.

Spot Solana ETFs lost $32.1 million last week, per SoSoValue, their sixth straight negative week and the longest such run since the funds launched in October 2025. The outflow streak began the same week the funds snapped a record 14-week inflow run, and it has drained $197.4 million since.

The Solana funds posted outflows in every session last week, extending their daily losing streak to seven days. Fidelity's FSOL accounted for all of Friday's $3.1 million outflow. Net assets fell to $1.14 billion from $1.31 billion a week earlier, though, unlike their BTC and ETH brethren, the funds remain about $644.1 million positive for the year.

Grayscale's Zcash fund, ZCSH, the only U.S. spot Zcash ETF, lost $30.7 million, nearly as much as the nine Solana funds combined, per SoSoValue. It was the fund's second straight negative week, and the outflow matched an early-October week as its largest since late September. ZCSH's net assets fell 32% over the week to $523.7 million.

Spot XRP ETFs shed $19.1 million, per SoSoValue, their largest weekly outflow since mid-March and a second straight negative week. Most of it left on Monday and Tuesday, at $10.4 million and $7.6 million, respectively. On Friday, Grayscale's GXRP lost $5.5 million while Franklin's XRPZ took in $4.5 million.

The three U.S. Hyperliquid ETFs lost $4.3 million, extending their weekly outflow streak to six, the longest since they began trading in May, per SoSoValue. Smaller funds tracking NEAR, Chainlink, Hedera and Polkadot lost between $99,000 and $1.4 million each. The BNB, Dogecoin, Tron and Litecoin funds reported no flows for the week.

The Avalanche funds’ modest $227,000 inflow on Thursday, their only day with any net flows, formed the only black in a sea of red last week.
